title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
順天府鄉試錄序
國朝設鄉試之科三載一開已成
故事蓋自我
太祖高皇帝定都應天建學立師裁
訂品式而其制已備
太宗文皇帝遷都順天表章經書頒
示天下學校而其制益詳
===
列聖繼繼承承敬守不怠迨我
皇上任賢使能治有成績益慎益崇
故
詔旨嘗曰學校事重提學官其振
揚風紀嚴督教條務期成效大哉
皇言天下士子聞之莫不競相濯磨
以求無負矧

punctuated:
順天府鄉試錄序

國朝設鄉試之科，三載一開，已成故事。蓋自我太祖高皇帝定都應天，建學立師，裁訂品式，而其制已備。太宗文皇帝遷都順天，表章經書，頒示天下學校，而其制益詳。列聖繼繼承承，敬守不怠。迨我皇上任賢使能，治有成績，益慎益崇。故詔旨嘗曰：「學校事重，提學官其振揚風紀，嚴督教條，務期成效。」大哉皇言！天下士子聞之，莫不競相濯磨，以求無負。矧
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Our dynasty established the Provincial Examination, held once every three years, and this has become settled precedent. When our Emperor Gao, Taizu, established his capital at Yingtian, founded schools, appointed teachers, and determined standards and procedures, the system was already complete. Emperor Wen, Taizong, moved the capital to Shuntian, gave prominence to the canonical books, and promulgated them to schools throughout the realm, making the system still more detailed. Successive sage emperors continued this inheritance, reverently preserving it without flagging. Under our present emperor, who appoints the worthy and employs the capable, government has achieved results, and still greater care and esteem have been accorded to this system.

Thus an imperial edict once declared: “The affairs of schools are of great importance. Let the education intendants uphold discipline, rigorously enforce the regulations for instruction, and make every effort to achieve results.” How great are these imperial words! Upon hearing them, scholars throughout the realm have without exception vied to cleanse and refine themselves, seeking not to fall short of these expectations. How much more so…

translation_en:
…how much more so the scholars of the capital region, who dwell close beneath the imperial carriage and are the first to hear and see these things!
This autumn, the time again came to hold the examination. Your servant Wang Ding, Prefect of Shuntian, and his colleagues obtained permission to conduct it according to established precedent. His Majesty entrusted the duties of Examiner to your servants Fu Gui, Academician, and Mao Cheng, Expositor-in-waiting. The Associate Examiners were your servants Zhang Xian, Lin Fang, and Yao Liang, Professors; Cheng Mei, Ning Qin, Hou Ji, Chen Xun, and Wu Datian, Instructors; and Zheng Shao, Assistant Instructor. The examination was overseen by your servants Li Tingwu and Yuan Xuan, Investigating Censors. The Proctor was the aforementioned Prefect, your servant Wang Ding.

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
制得中式者百三十有五人尚多
可取而止於此者亦
制也簡其文之尤純者得二十篇
合爲錄一編以
獻臣珪當序諸首竊惟科目所以

===

焉耳故有菁莪棫樸之化而後
有有德有造之賢有鎬京辟雝
之教而後獲保有厥士之用然

朝名臣碩輔相望於後先科目之

制，得中式者百三十有五人，尚多可取而止於此者，亦制也。簡其文之尤純者，得二十篇，合爲錄一編以獻。臣珪當序諸首。
竊惟科目所以取士，學校所以養士，然必養之既充，而後乃可取而用之也。鄧林之木，小大畢材，亦惟得其養焉耳。故有菁莪、棫樸之化，而後有有德有造之賢；有鎬京、辟雝之教，而後獲保有厥士之用。然則我朝名臣碩輔，相望於後先，科目之英尤盛於
translation_en:
…in accordance with the regulations, 135 candidates passed. Many more were worthy of selection, but the number stopped here because this too was prescribed by regulation. Twenty essays of especially fine quality were selected and compiled into a single examination record for presentation to the throne. Your servant Gui was charged with placing a preface at its beginning.
I humbly reflect that the examination system serves to select men of talent, while schools serve to nurture them. Only after they have been fully nurtured can they be selected and employed. The trees of Deng Forest, large and small alike, all become useful timber simply because they receive proper nourishment. Thus, only with the transforming influence celebrated in “Luxuriant Southernwood” (Jing e) and “Oak and Thorn” (Yu pu) do worthy men of virtue and accomplishment emerge; only with the instruction exemplified by Haojing and the royal academy (biyong) can the benefit of “retaining its men of talent” be secured. title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
今日者抑豈偶然之故哉歲丁卯
臣嘗承乏主應天之試親見其
所謂盛者既畢試則謁廟詣學
又獲見洪武中養賢之具雖至
纖至微罔不精密臣於是仰而
嘆曰是惡可不知所自邪初順
天之地藩省在焉取士之額纔
===
四十人而止既而進為
京府其士額亦漸進與應天等及
今又數十年又被我
皇上維新之化是宜人才之又進也
臣於不能盡錄之餘復仰而嘆
曰是又惡可不知所自邪由
兩京達之天下相觀而興彬彬濟

天之地藩省在焉取士之額纔
===
四十人而止既而進為
京府其士額亦漸進與應天等及
今又數十年又被我
皇上維新之化是宜人才之又進也
臣
於不能盡錄之餘復仰而嘆
曰是又惡可不知所自邪由
兩京達之天下相觀而興彬彬濟
punctuated:
今日者，抑豈偶然之故哉？歲丁卯，臣嘗承乏主應天之試，親見其所謂盛者。既畢試，則謁廟詣學，又獲見洪武中養賢之具，雖至纖至微，罔不精密。臣於是仰而嘆曰：「是惡可不知所自邪？」

初，順天之地，藩省在焉，取士之額纔四十人而止。既而進為京府，其士額亦漸進，與應天等。及今又數十年，又被我皇上維新之化，是宜人才之又進也。臣於不能盡錄之餘，復仰而嘆曰：「是又惡可不知所自邪？」由兩京達之天下，相觀而興，彬彬濟
translation_en:
…today—could this possibly have come about by mere chance? In the dingmao year (1507), your servant had the honor, despite his inadequacy, of presiding over the examination at Yingtian and personally witnessed this flourishing of talent. After the examination was completed, I paid my respects at the temple and visited the school. There I also saw the provisions made during the Hongwu reign for nurturing worthy men: even the smallest details were meticulously arranged. I thereupon looked up and sighed: “How can we fail to recognize the source of this?”

Originally, Shuntian was the seat of a provincial administration, and its quota for selecting candidates was only forty. After it was elevated to a capital prefecture, its quota gradually increased until it equaled that of Yingtian. Several more decades have now passed, and it has further benefited from the renewing influence of our emperor. It is fitting, therefore, that its talent should advance still further. Unable to record everything, your servant again looked up and sighed: “How, again, can we fail to recognize the source of this?” Extending from the two capitals throughout the realm, men take inspiration from one another and rise to achievement, cultured and numerous…

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:

盡於今皆不可不知所自也昔
大雅詩人歌文王之德則叙其
遷豐之事歌武王之德則叙其
遷鎬之事而迨如兩漢其臣亦
有為兩都賦以頌美之者我

鋪張揚厲以風示天下豈不有

命而來不遑寢食惟以取士不得

punctuated: 濟，或漸增其額於昔，或額不能盡於今，皆不可不知所自也。昔《大雅》詩人歌文王之德，則叙其遷豐之事；歌武王之德，則叙其遷鎬之事。而迨如兩漢，其臣亦有為《兩都賦》以頌美之者。我聖祖神宗豐芑之詒，暨列聖皇上繼述之大，臣幸與聞之，乃不能鋪張揚厲，以風示天下，豈不有負於明時矣乎？雖然，臣等奉命而來，不遑寢食，惟以取士不得
translation_en: …in flourishing abundance. In some places the quotas have gradually increased over those of former times; in others even the present quotas cannot be filled. In every case, one must understand the source of these circumstances. Formerly, when the poets of the Greater Odes praised King Wen’s virtue, they recounted his move to Feng; when they praised King Wu’s virtue, they recounted his move to Hao. Later, under the two Han dynasties, there were likewise ministers who composed works such as the Rhapsody on the Two Capitals to celebrate their splendor. Your servant has been fortunate to learn of the legacy of nurturing future generations bequeathed by our sagely founder and divine ancestors, and of the greatness with which the successive sage sovereigns and Your Majesty have carried forward their work. If I cannot expound and extol these achievements so as to instruct all under Heaven, would I not be failing this enlightened age? Nevertheless, we, your servants, have come in obedience to your command, with no leisure for sleep or meals, concerned only lest, in selecting men, we fail to obtain…

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
為憂顧今所錄者若皆養之有
成者也若皆才之美而有用者
也苟可以梁可以棟者果出於
其間應
廟堂匠石之選答
九重求材之意焉是亦臣等所以
圖報於萬一而又藉以自慶自
===
慰者也
翰林院學士奉議大夫傅珪謹
序
alt_text:
為憂頎今所錄者若干皆養之有
成者也若皆才之美而有用者
也苟可以澀可以棟者果出於
其間應
廟堂匠石之選答
九重求材之意焉是亦〔臣〕等所以
圖報於萬一而又藉以自慶自
===
慰者也
翰林院學士奉議大夫傅珪謹
序
punctuated:
為憂。顧今所錄者，若皆養之有成者也，若皆才之美而有用者也。苟可以梁、可以棟者果出於其間，應廟堂匠石之選，答九重求材之意焉，是亦臣等所以圖報於萬一，而又藉以自慶自慰者也。
翰林院學士、奉議大夫傅珪謹序。
translation_en:
…as our concern. Yet those now selected seem all to have brought their cultivation to fruition, and all to possess fine talents suited to practical use. If men fit to serve as beams and ridgepoles indeed emerge from among them, meeting the court’s master craftsmen’s criteria for selection and answering His Majesty’s desire to obtain worthy talent, this too will be a means by which we, your servants, may hope to repay one ten-thousandth of the imperial favor, and may find cause for congratulation and consolation.
Preface respectfully composed by Fu Gui, Academician of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Deliberation (fengyi dafu).

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
生財有大道生之者衆食之者寡爲之者
疾用之者舒則財恒足矣
仕而優則學學而優則仕
尊賢使能俊傑在位則天下之士皆悅而
願立於其朝矣
易
君子以成德爲行日可見之行也
===
益動而巽日進无疆天施地生其益无方
天尊地卑乾坤定矣卑高以陳貴賤位矣
動靜有常剛柔斷矣方以類聚物以羣
分吉凶生矣在天成象在地成形變化
見矣是故剛柔相摩八卦相盪鼓之以
雷霆潤之以風雨日月運行一寒一暑
乾道成男坤道成女
聚而上者謂之升故受之以升

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

生財有大道：生之者衆，食之者寡，爲之者疾，用之者舒，則財恒足矣。

仕而優則學，學而優則仕。

尊賢使能，俊傑在位，則天下之士皆悅而願立於其朝矣。

易

君子以成德爲行，日可見之行也。

益，動而巽，日進无疆。天施地生，其益无方。

天尊地卑，乾坤定矣。卑高以陳，貴賤位矣。動靜有常，剛柔斷矣。方以類聚，物以羣分，吉凶生矣。在天成象，在地成形，變化見矣。是故剛柔相摩，八卦相盪。鼓之以雷霆，潤之以風雨。日月運行，一寒一暑。乾道成男，坤道成女。

聚而上者謂之升，故受之以升。

書
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

There is a great way to produce wealth: let those who produce it be many and those who consume it few; let those who produce it work swiftly and those who use it spend slowly. Then wealth will always be sufficient.

When serving in office, if you have capacity to spare, study; when studying, if you have capacity to spare, serve in office.

Honor the worthy and employ the capable, placing outstanding men in office; then all the scholars of the realm will rejoice and wish to stand at your court.

Book of Changes (Yi)

The gentleman makes perfected virtue the basis of his conduct; this is conduct that can be seen day by day.

Increase: movement combined with yielding brings daily advance without limit. Heaven bestows and earth brings forth; their increase knows no bounds.

Heaven is exalted and earth is lowly; thus Qian and Kun are established. Low and high are arrayed; thus the positions of noble and base are determined. Movement and stillness have their constant patterns; thus the firm and the yielding are distinguished. Things come together according to their kinds, and creatures divide into groups; thus good fortune and misfortune arise. In heaven, images take shape; on earth, forms take shape; thus change and transformation become manifest. Therefore the firm and the yielding rub against each other, and the eight trigrams stir one another. They are roused by thunder and thunderbolts and moistened by wind and rain. The sun and moon follow their courses, with cold and heat alternating. The way of Qian brings forth the male; the way of Kun brings forth the female.

Gathering together and moving upward is called Ascending; therefore it is followed by the hexagram Ascending (Sheng).

Book of Documents (Shu)

平章百姓，百姓昭明，協和萬邦，黎民於變時雍。

爾惟訓于朕志。若作酒醴，爾惟麴蘖；若作和羹，爾惟鹽梅。爾交修予，罔予棄，予惟克邁乃訓。

庸庸，祗祗，威威，顯民，用肇造我區夏，越我一二邦，以修我西土。惟時怙冒，聞于上帝。

詩

婉兮孌兮，總角丱兮！未幾見兮，突而弁兮！

左之左之，君子宜之；右之右之，君子有之。維其有之，是以似之。

鎬京辟廱，自西自東，自南自北，無思不服。皇王烝哉！

帝命式于九圍。

春秋

宋公、陳侯、蔡人、衛人伐鄭。會宋公、陳侯
translation_en:
He made equitable distinctions among the hundred clans. Once the hundred clans were enlightened, he brought the myriad states into harmony, and the common people were transformed and became harmonious.

You must instruct my mind. If I were making wine or sweet liquor, you would be the yeast and malt; if I were making a well-seasoned broth, you would be the salt and sour plums. Correct me in every respect; do not abandon me. I shall indeed follow your instruction.

The first is called the Five Elements; the second is called the reverent exercise of the Five Affairs.

They employed those worthy of employment, honored those worthy of honor, awed those deserving of awe, and distinguished the people. Thus they first established our realm of Xia and, together with our few allied states, brought order to our western lands. This protection and shelter became known to the Lord on High.

Songs

How graceful, how lovely, with the hair tied in two hornlike tufts! After only a short time without seeing him, suddenly he wears an adult’s cap!

To the left, to the left: the gentleman moves fittingly. To the right, to the right: the gentleman possesses the skill. Because he possesses it, he is emulated.

At the royal academy in Haojing, from the west and from the east, from the south and from the north, none failed to submit. How august was the king!

The Lord on High commanded him to serve as a model throughout the nine regions.

Spring and Autumn Annals

The Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, and men of Cai and Wei attacked Zheng. [The Duke] joined the Duke of Song and the Marquis of Chen …

“Observing one another and thereby improving is called mutual polishing.”

“Music is the harmony of Heaven and Earth; ritual is the order of Heaven and Earth. Through harmony, all things undergo transformation; through order, all things are distinguished.”

地民物之詳為安擾邦國之計若書之

矣或分天下為十二州或制為九州或

Question: Whenever a dynasty arises, it must have a gazetteer of its own, recording in detail its lands, people, and products, to provide a basis for plans to pacify and govern the realm. The “Tribute of Yu” (Yu gong) in the Book of Documents and the responsibilities of the Minister of Education in the Rites of Zhou are both examples of this. Thus, at the founding of our state, Emperor Taizu Gao immediately ordered several Confucian scholars to compile and classify geographical information about the realm and make a gazetteer of it. After establishing the capital, Emperor Taizong Wen immediately dispatched officials on separate journeys throughout the realm to gather factual information and make a book of it. Were that gazetteer and that book completed or not? What can you tell us about them?

The Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Ming (Da Ming yitong zhi) was compiled during the reign of our Emperor Yingzong. Its principles of organization and categories are lucid, and no place is too remote to be recorded: it may be called a supremely flourishing achievement. Yet did it indeed originate in the sovereign’s own distinctive insight, or did it carry forward the intentions of his imperial ancestors?

From the times of Tang Yao and Yu Shun onward, many have claimed to unify the realm. Some divided all under Heaven into twelve provinces, others organized it into nine provinces; some had more than three thousand states, others eighteen hundred. Compared with the territory united under our dynasty, which was truly greater? From the Han and Tang onward, many have compiled geographical records. 問：《論語》言仁最詳。夫子許雍可南面，由可賦，求可宰，赤可賓客，而皆不許其仁，獨稱顔子三月不違。顔子死，曾子傳夫子之道，其言曰：「仁以爲己任。」不知二子之學，其所以異於羣弟子者何如，而所造乃如此？且夫子平居所以答門弟子問仁者，大抵皆仁之用與夫求仁之方，而言各不同，何也？至若稱微子、箕子、比干爲三仁，伯夷、叔齊爲得仁，其於令尹子文之忠、陳文子之清，則皆曰：「未知，焉得仁？」嘗以器小譏管仲矣，他日答子路之
translation_en:
…compared with our dynasty’s geographical record, which is more comprehensive? The preface at the beginning of the record was itself written by the imperial hand and shines as brightly as the sun and stars. It contains words admonishing the emperor’s sagely sons and divine grandsons and encouraging his subjects. Can the imperial intent behind these words also be explained in detail? You candidates pursue learning through broad knowledge of antiquity and understanding of the present; surely you have long reverently studied the books of the present dynasty. Respond respectfully, without holding back.
Question: The Analects discusses benevolence in the greatest detail. The Master acknowledged that Yong could occupy the ruler’s south-facing seat, that You could administer military levies, that Qiu could serve as a steward, and that Chi could receive guests, yet he would not acknowledge any of them as benevolent. Only of Master Yan did he say that for three months he did not depart from benevolence. After Master Yan died, Master Zeng transmitted the Master’s Way, saying, “Take benevolence as one’s own responsibility.” In what respects did the learning of these two differ from that of the other disciples, such that their attainments reached this level? Furthermore, when the Master ordinarily answered his disciples’ questions about benevolence, his replies generally concerned its practical application or the methods of seeking it. Why, then, did his words differ in each case? He called Weizi, Jizi, and Bi Gan the three benevolent men, and said that Bo Yi and Shu Qi had attained benevolence. 問，再言「如其仁」，又若有深許之者。既曰「克己復禮為仁」，及答原憲之問，則但以克伐怨慾不行為難，而不以為仁。若此者，其大旨何居？夫子沒而微言絕，由漢而下，儒者若董子、韓子皆不識仁。迨宋程朱氏出，而後仁之說始精，聖門之教由是復明於世，其大要可得聞歟？程氏之徒，有謂愛非仁，而以萬物與我為一為仁之體者，此似立人達人之仁也；有謂愛非仁，而以心有知覺釋仁之名者，此似可逝不可陷、可欺不可罔之仁也。何朱子皆不取，而云其弊將至於認物為己、認欲為理乎？諸生苟有志於求仁，其必不惑於斯矣。
問：先儒有言：「天下有三本，師教之其一也。」故雖聖賢，莫不有師，而所謂教者，莫不有法。試與諸生論之：或以天縱之聖，而猶問禮問官；或以亞聖之次，而有所願
translation_en:
…inquiry, he twice said, “Who could equal his benevolence?” seemingly expressing profound approval of him. Having said, “Overcoming oneself and returning to ritual propriety constitutes benevolence,” when answering Yuan Xian’s question he merely treated refraining from competitiveness, boasting, resentment, and desire as difficult, without regarding it as benevolence. What is the main purport of such statements? After the Master died, his subtle teachings were lost. From the Han onward, scholars such as Master Dong and Master Han failed to understand benevolence. Only with the emergence of the Cheng masters and Master Zhu in the Song did explanations of benevolence become precise, and the teachings of the sage’s school thereby became clear to the world once more. May we hear their essential points? Among the followers of the Cheng masters, some maintained that love is not benevolence and regarded the unity of the myriad things with oneself as the substance of benevolence. This seems akin to the benevolence of helping others establish themselves and attain their goals. Others maintained that love is not benevolence and explained the term “benevolence” through the mind’s capacity for awareness. This seems akin to the benevolence of one who may be induced to go but cannot be entrapped, who may be deceived but cannot be wholly deluded. Why did Master Zhu reject both explanations, saying that their errors would lead to mistaking external things for oneself and desire for principle? If you students are intent on seeking benevolence, surely you will not be confused about these matters.
Question: An earlier Confucian scholar said, “There are three foundations of the realm; instruction by teachers is one of them.” Thus even sages and worthies invariably had teachers, and what is called teaching invariably had its methods. Let us discuss this with you students. One, though a sage endowed by Heaven, still asked about rites and official offices; another, though ranking as the Second Sage, had something he wished to…

text:
學受業或曰弟子不必不如師師不必
賢於弟子或曰愈旣自以爲蜀之日吾
子又欲使吾爲越之雪默契道體者或
謂不由師傳或謂始有所學洞見道體
者或歸功於吟風弄月或推本於博聞
强記或以虎皮爲坐者已即師席矣何
所聞而即撤去或奉父命禀學者歸自
同安矣何所聞而又徒歩以徃此皆師
道之見於載籍者其間亦有得失之可
===
言歟求之孔門古今所共遵而不可易
之説又當以何者爲準歟周禮師氏之
教或以三德或以三行其教異歟諸儒
之論教也或以禮爲先或以立志爲先
或以恭謹爲先或以知止爲先或以訓
詁文義爲先或以逐小忘大爲玩物喪
志此皆教法之見於載籍者其間亦有
得失之可言歟求之孔門古今所共由
而不可易之法又當以何者爲準歟夫

translation_en: …to study and receive instruction. One said: “A disciple need not be inferior to his teacher, nor need a teacher be worthier than his disciple.” Another said: “I, Yu, already consider myself the sun of Shu, yet you would also have me become the snow of Yue.” Of one who tacitly apprehended the substance of the Way, some say that his understanding did not come through a teacher’s transmission, while others say that he first received instruction. Of one who clearly perceived the substance of the Way, some credit chanting of the wind and enjoying the moon, while others trace his achievement to extensive learning and a powerful memory. One who used a tiger skin as his seat had already assumed the teacher’s place: what did he hear that caused him immediately to remove it? Another, who sought instruction at his father’s command, had returned from Tong’an: what did he hear that caused him to go again on foot? These are all instances of the way of teachers recorded in written sources. Are there successes and failings among them that can be discussed? Looking to the school of Confucius, which teaching should we take as the standard, observed alike in antiquity and today and admitting of no alteration? In the Rites of Zhou, the instruction given by the Preceptor concerns, in one instance, the Three Virtues and, in another, the Three Forms of Conduct. Do these teachings differ? In discussing education, some Confucian scholars give priority to ritual propriety; others to setting one’s resolve; others to reverence and circumspection; others to knowing where to rest; and others to textual glosses and the meaning of passages. Still others regard pursuing the small and forgetting the great as becoming engrossed in things and losing one’s resolve. These are all methods of teaching recorded in written sources. Are there successes and failings among them that can be discussed? title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
成己成物皆儒者事其明著于篇俾為
師者知所以教為弟子者知所以學
問設官分職凡以為民也程子獨以斯民
之休戚係於守令之賢否何所見歟有
曰太守吏民之本有曰郡守縣令民之
師帥其於程子之論果同歟守令之重
如此顧其為政有不可不慎焉者寬則
得衆寬若可以為政矣然又曰嚴之則
治寬之則亂乃不取於寬歟其次莫如
===
猛猛若可以服民矣然又曰治亂民猶
治亂繩不可急也豈不足於猛歟求之
於古有獨用寬和者有但用蒲鞭者有
教以禮義者有專以德化者果皆得政
體歟有郡中震栗者有吏民改行者有
稱為神筭者有目為卧虎者果皆得民
心歟
聖朝之賢守令多矣迨弘治末時則以寬為尚
犯者未必罪罪者未必盡逋稅或姑息

punctuated:
成己成物，皆儒者事。其明著于篇，俾為師者知所以教，為弟子者知所以學。

問：設官分職，凡以為民也。程子獨以斯民之休戚係於守令之賢否，何所見歟？有曰：「太守，吏民之本。」有曰：「郡守縣令，民之師帥。」其於程子之論果同歟？守令之重如此，顧其為政，有不可不慎焉者。「寬則得衆」，寬若可以為政矣；然又曰：「嚴之則治，寬之則亂。」乃不取於寬歟？「其次莫如猛」，猛若可以服民矣；然又曰：「治亂民猶治亂繩，不可急也。」豈不足於猛歟？求之於古，有獨用寬和者，有但用蒲鞭者，有教以禮義者，有專以德化者，果皆得政體歟？有郡中震栗者，有吏民改行者，有稱為神筭者，有目為卧虎者，果皆得民心歟？聖朝之賢守令多矣。迨弘治末時，則以寬為尚，犯者未必罪，罪者未必盡，逋稅或姑息
translation_en:
…Perfecting oneself and bringing others to fulfillment are both the work of the Confucian scholar. Set these matters out clearly in your essay, so that teachers may know how to teach and disciples how to learn.

Question: Establishing offices and dividing responsibilities are all for the sake of the people. Master Cheng, however, held that the well-being or suffering of the people depended specifically upon whether prefects and county magistrates were worthy. What insight underlay this view? One statement says, “The prefect is the foundation upon which officials and people depend.” Another says, “Prefects and county magistrates are the people’s teachers and leaders.” Do these indeed accord with Master Cheng’s argument? Such is the importance of prefects and magistrates; yet in governing there are matters in which they must exercise particular care. “With leniency one wins the multitude”: leniency would thus seem suitable for governing. Yet it is also said, “Treat them strictly and there is order; treat them leniently and there is disorder.” Does this mean that leniency is not approved? “The next best course is severity”: severity would thus seem capable of securing the people’s submission. Yet it is also said, “Governing disorderly people is like untangling tangled cord: one must not hurry.” Does this suggest that severity is inadequate? Looking to antiquity, some relied exclusively on leniency and gentleness; some used only whips made of rushes; some instructed the people in ritual propriety and righteousness; and some relied entirely on moral transformation. Did all of them truly grasp the proper principles of government? Some made their entire prefecture tremble; some brought officials and people to reform their conduct; some were praised for their uncanny calculation; and some were called crouching tigers. Did all of them truly win the people’s hearts? Our sagely dynasty has had many worthy prefects and magistrates. By the end of the Hongzhi reign, however, leniency had become the favored approach. Offenders were not necessarily punished, nor were all those liable to punishment necessarily dealt with; tax arrears were sometimes indulgently tolerated…

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而不徵部檄或因循而不報民竟有萑
符之取者何歟承寛之後邇乃有以嚴
爲尚者矣犯者未嘗不罪罪者未嘗不
盡逋税雖已往而必徵部檄及始下而
擬報民又有潢池之擾者何歟將惟寛
是欲則今日之事可懲將惟嚴是戒則
前日之患未息伊欲寛以御之而不失
之縱嚴以治之而不失之刻俾小民享
和平之福
===
盛世成雍熈之化如之何則可
問禹抑洪水其言養民之政水實居六府
先蓋水之於民有利有害使民得去其
害而就其利顧不在人事乎今瀕河州
郡恒苦河决而吳中多水患求之人事
豈無可為者昔人謂自西漢河入千乗
訖東都至唐不為患者千數百年方兩
浙未歸宋鮮聞水患自宋一統之後賊
毎不充此其故何也我

punctuated:
而不徵，部檄或因循而不報，民竟有萑符之取者，何歟？承寛之後，邇乃有以嚴爲尚者矣。犯者未嘗不罪，罪者未嘗不盡；逋税雖已往而必徵，部檄及始下而擬報，民又有潢池之擾者，何歟？將惟寛是欲，則今日之事可懲；將惟嚴是戒，則前日之患未息。伊欲寛以御之而不失之縱，嚴以治之而不失之刻，俾小民享和平之福，盛世成雍熈之化，如之何則可？

問：禹抑洪水，其言養民之政，水實居六府先。蓋水之於民，有利有害，使民得去其害而就其利，顧不在人事乎？今瀕河州郡恒苦河决，而吳中多水患，求之人事，豈無可為者？昔人謂，自西漢河入千乗，訖東都至唐，不為患者千數百年。方兩浙未歸宋，鮮聞水患；自宋一統之後，賊毎不充，此其故何也？我
translation_en:
…and are not collected; dispatches from the ministries are sometimes left unanswered through procrastination. Yet some among the people have resorted to plunder in the marshes [?]. Why is this? Following this period of leniency, some have recently come to favor severity. No offender goes unpunished, and punishments are invariably exacted in full. Tax arrears are collected even when long overdue, and replies to ministerial dispatches are drafted as soon as they arrive. Yet disturbances among the people have again arisen, like rebels taking up arms by stagnant pools. Why is this? If leniency alone is sought, present events offer a warning; if severity alone is guarded against, the troubles of former days remain unresolved. We wish to govern with leniency without lapsing into laxity, and to rule with severity without lapsing into harshness, so that ordinary people may enjoy the blessings of peace and harmony, and this flourishing age may achieve harmonious and glorious transformation. How can this be accomplished?

Question: Yu checked the floodwaters, and in his account of government that sustains the people, water stood first among the Six Resources. Water can benefit the people or harm them. Does not enabling them to avoid its harm and obtain its benefits depend upon human effort? Today, prefectures and subprefectures along the Yellow River constantly suffer from breaches in its banks, while the Wu region frequently experiences flooding. If we look to human effort, is there really nothing that can be done? Earlier writers said that, from the time the Yellow River entered Qiansheng in the Western Han, through the Eastern Han and down to the Tang, it caused no calamities for more than a thousand years. Before the Two Zhe regions came under Song rule, floods were seldom reported; after the Song unified the realm, ‘bandits were repeatedly insufficient’ [?]. What accounts for this? Our…

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
朝建國幽燕漕東南之粟以實京師必由濟
博之境故河决而東則漕渠失利其害
非獨在民而三吳之地歲所出
國家財賦當天下半其所繫豈輕也哉茲欲
修漢賈讓關並韓牧之策治今之决河
用宋郟亶單鍔趙霖之議求今之水利
其參酌利害以對任養民之職者亦將
有擇於斯也

punctuated: 朝建國幽燕，漕東南之粟以實京師，必由濟、博之境，故河决而東，則漕渠失利。其害非獨在民，而三吳之地，歲所出國家財賦當天下半，其所繫豈輕也哉！茲欲修漢賈讓、關並、韓牧之策，治今之决河；用宋郟亶、單鍔、趙霖之議，求今之水利。其參酌利害以對，任養民之職者亦將有擇於斯也。
translation_en:
…our dynasty established its capital in Youyan. Grain from the southeast is transported by water to provision the capital and must pass through the territories of Ji and Bo. Thus, when the Yellow River breaches its banks and flows eastward, the grain-transport canal loses its usefulness. The harm does not affect the people alone. Moreover, the annual tax revenues supplied to the state by the Three Wu region amount to half those of the empire. Can the interests at stake be considered slight?

We now wish to put into practice the plans of Jia Rang, Guan Bing, and Han Mu [?] of the Han dynasty to control the present breaches of the Yellow River, and to apply the proposals of Jia Dan, Shan E, and Zhao Lin of the Song dynasty to secure benefits from water today. Weigh their advantages and disadvantages in your reply. Those charged with nourishing the people will also find here measures from which to choose.

The 135 successful provincial graduates (juren).

First: Wang Jiang, a native of Renqiu County, Zhili, and a student of the Directorate of Education. His examination classic was the Book of Odes. He is also marked as a metropolitan graduate (jinshi).

Third: Xu Ren, a government student of Jiaohe County, Zhili. His examination classic was the Book of Changes.

Fourth: Peng Xu, a native of Liyang County, Yingtian Prefecture, and a student of the Directorate of Education. His examination classic was the Record of Rites.

Tenth: Gao Xuan, a supplementary student at the Shuntian Prefectural School. His examination subject is garbled as 嵗六書 [?]. He is also marked as a metropolitan graduate (jinshi).

Thirteenth: Zhang Yunqu, a government student of Pinggu County, Shuntian Prefecture. His examination classic was the Book of Odes.

First Session
Four Books
“There is a great way to produce wealth: let those who produce it be many and those who consume it few; let those who make it work swiftly and those who use it spend slowly. Then wealth will always be sufficient.”
Wang Han

Comment by Associate Examiner Hou, Instructor: “The commentary and annotations make this topic clear in themselves. Most candidates writing in the examination hall become entangled in their treatment, displeasing both mind and eye. This essay is rich and elegant yet exhaustive in meaning, rigorous and lucid yet clear in principle. Record it.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Ning, Instructor: “The topic is inherently plain and straightforward. Many candidates indulge excessively in flights of composition, producing instead something tiresomely verbose and convoluted. This work is concise and clear, detailed and comprehensive. It is therefore recorded as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Qian, Academician Expositor-in-waiting: “The language is not verbose, and the meaning closely addresses the topic. In expounding the meaning of the Great Learning, no essay surpasses this one.”

Comment by Examiner Fu, Academician: “The wording and purport are orderly and clean. It merits recording.”

The Great Learning says that there is a great way to manage wealth, and that for those able to follow this way, wealth will naturally be abundant. In managing wealth, nothing is more important than attending to the root and exercising restraint in expenditure. If one can indeed follow this way, why worry that wealth will not be abundant? The tenth chapter of the commentary to the Great Learning, in discussing how possession of territory brings possession of wealth, develops its explanation in these terms. title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
民者非財乎長國家者欲使生生不已則自有
正大之道豈必厲民而自養哉取諸貢賦以資
國者非財乎有天下者欲使源源不竭則自有
公平之道豈必損下而益上哉盖必於其入也
務生之為之之本而於其出也謹食之用之之
節則其道得矣生之寡而食之者衆是相率而
為怠且奢也財烏乎不匱今也田蠶貨賄家無
遺力國無閒民則生之衆矣視諸其朝凡建官
制禄必選賢能而無尸素之位斯不亦食之者
===
寡乎為之舒而用之者疾是舉國而違勤與儉
也利烏乎不屈今也師田力役不奪農時不妨
稼事則為之疾矣稽之在公雖匪頒好用亦存
品式而無泛濫之費斯不亦用之者舒乎夫既
能務本以開財之源而又能儉用以節財之流
則其来無窮其去有限故倉廪常豐雖加之以
師旅不至窘於調度矣府庫常盈雖因之以饑
饉不至迫於費用矣是固非以私意小智巧為
聚斂之術而致然也謂之曰大道不亦宜乎嗟

punctuated: 民者，非財乎？長國家者欲使生生不已，則自有正大之道，豈必厲民而自養哉？取諸貢賦以資國者，非財乎？有天下者欲使源源不竭，則自有公平之道，豈必損下而益上哉？盖必於其入也，務生之為之之本；而於其出也，謹食之用之之節，則其道得矣。生之寡而食之者衆，是相率而為怠且奢也，財烏乎不匱？今也田蠶貨賄，家無遺力，國無閒民，則生之衆矣。視諸其朝，凡建官制禄，必選賢能，而無尸素之位，斯不亦食之者寡乎？為之舒而用之者疾，是舉國而違勤與儉也，利烏乎不屈？今也師田力役，不奪農時，不妨稼事，則為之疾矣。稽之在公，雖匪頒好用，亦存品式，而無泛濫之費，斯不亦用之者舒乎？夫既能務本以開財之源，而又能儉用以節財之流，則其来無窮，其去有限。故倉廪常豐，雖加之以師旅，不至窘於調度矣；府庫常盈，雖因之以饑饉，不至迫於費用矣。是固非以私意小智巧為聚斂之術而致然也，謂之曰大道，不亦宜乎？嗟
translation_en:
…the people—is this not wealth? Those who preside over the state and its ruling houses, wishing to ensure that production continues without end, have an upright and great way to follow. Why must they oppress the people to support themselves? What is collected through tribute and taxation to sustain the state—is this not wealth? Those who possess all under Heaven, wishing to ensure an inexhaustible flow, have a fair and impartial way to follow. Why must they diminish those below to enrich those above?

In receiving wealth, they must attend to its foundations in production and productive work; in disbursing it, they must carefully regulate its consumption and use. Then they will have attained the proper way. If those who produce it are few and those who consume it are many, they are leading one another into idleness and extravagance. How could wealth fail to run short? But if, in farming, sericulture, and the production of goods, no household spares its efforts and the state has no idle people, then its producers will be many. Looking to the court, if every establishment of offices and provision of salaries entails selecting the worthy and capable, with no posts occupied by those who draw salaries without performing their duties, will its consumers not be few?

If production is slow and expenditure rapid, the whole state is departing from diligence and frugality. How could its resources fail to be exhausted? But if military expeditions, hunts, and labor service neither encroach upon the farming seasons nor impede cultivation, then production will be rapid. Examining public expenditure, if even distributions and expenditures on gifts of goodwill [?] observe prescribed grades and rules, without unchecked spending, will expenditure not be slow?

If they can attend to the foundations and thereby open the sources of wealth, while also practicing frugality and thereby regulating its outflow, its inflow will be inexhaustible and its outflow limited. Thus the granaries will always be well stocked: even when military operations impose additional burdens, there will be no difficulty in arranging supplies. The treasuries will always be full: even when famine follows, there will be no pressure in meeting expenses. This certainly does not result from selfish intentions and petty cleverness ingeniously devising methods of extracting wealth. Is it not fitting to call it the great way? Alas…

text:

下足民有國之常政則又未嘗廢也其垂教後
世至矣當治平之任者其可忽諸
仕而優則學學而優則仕

translation_en:
…Among the eight concerns of government in the Great Plan, food and goods come first. When Zigong asked about government, the Master likewise began his reply with ensuring sufficient food. These are things that the people's livelihood cannot do without for even a single day: how could the sage take them lightly? The Great Learning discusses bringing peace to All under Heaven through the principle of the measuring square. Having just spoken of employing people, it proceeds to managing wealth. It shows the harm of treating the root as external and the branches as internal—that is, slighting virtue and valuing wealth—yet never sets aside the standing governmental duties of enriching those below and providing sufficiently for the people. How complete is its instruction for later generations! Can those charged with governing and bringing peace afford to neglect it?

“When service in office leaves strength to spare, study; when study leaves strength to spare, serve in office.”
Wang Jiang

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
盡其事而後及其餘哉昔子夏之意以為曰仕
曰學理雖同而事則異或仕或學力必專而功
可成是故上而為卿下而為士凡有官守者皆
仕也而仕則有仕之事焉致君澤民以佐理乎
萬幾陳力就列以分理乎庶職夙而興夜而寐
猶懼弗克於此而欲從事於學豈其時邪必也
政修教舉而萬幾之所佐者成心逸日休而庶
職之所分者理則其仕也有餘力矣夫然後誦
其詩讀其書以涵泳其所知也盡其心知其性
===
以敦篤其所能也仕優而學則既有以敬其仕
而不忽又有以資其仕而益深所謂仕者之於
學當知所先後蓋如此若夫始而致知終而力
行凡治吾身者皆學也而學則有學之事焉格
物窮理以辨析乎萬事誠意正心以求止於至
善如切磋如琢磨猶恐不及於此而欲從事於
仕豈其時邪必也知類通達而萬事之所析者
精強立不反而至善之所求者得則其學也有
餘力矣夫然後居其位食其禄以經綸於邦國

餘力矣夫然後居其位食其祿以經綸於邦國
punctuated:
盡其事而後及其餘哉？昔子夏之意以為：曰仕曰學，理雖同而事則異；或仕或學，力必專而功可成。是故上而為卿，下而為士，凡有官守者皆仕也，而仕則有仕之事焉。致君澤民，以佐理乎萬幾；陳力就列，以分理乎庶職。夙而興，夜而寐，猶懼弗克，於此而欲從事於學，豈其時邪？必也政修教舉，而萬幾之所佐者成；心逸日休，而庶職之所分者理，則其仕也有餘力矣。夫然後誦其詩，讀其書，以涵泳其所知也；盡其心，知其性，以敦篤其所能也。仕優而學，則既有以敬其仕而不忽，又有以資其仕而益深。所謂仕者之於學當知所先後，蓋如此。
若夫始而致知，終而力行，凡治吾身者皆學也，而學則有學之事焉。格物窮理，以辨析乎萬事；誠意正心，以求止於至善。如切磋，如琢磨，猶恐不及，於此而欲從事於仕，豈其時邪？必也知類通達，而萬事之所析者精；強立不反，而至善之所求者得，則其學也有餘力矣。夫然後居其位，食其禄，以經綸於邦國
translation_en:
…fulfill their own duties before turning to other matters? Zixia’s meaning was this: although holding office and learning share the same principle, their tasks differ. Whether one holds office or pursues learning, one must concentrate one’s efforts to achieve results. Thus, from ministers above to service gentlemen below, all who have official responsibilities are engaged in officeholding, and officeholding has its own tasks. They bring their ruler to perfection and confer benefits upon the people, assisting in the management of the myriad affairs of government; they take their places in the ranks according to their abilities, sharing responsibility for the many official duties. Rising early and retiring at night, they still fear that they cannot accomplish their work. Would this be the time to turn to learning? Only when government is well ordered and moral instruction promoted, so that their assistance in the myriad affairs has borne fruit; when their minds are at ease and their days unburdened, and the official duties allotted to them are properly managed—only then do they have energy to spare from officeholding. Then they recite the poems and read the writings, immersing themselves in what they know; they fully develop their minds and understand their nature, strengthening and deepening their capacities. To learn when one has energy to spare from officeholding both enables one to attend respectfully to official duties without neglect and provides resources that deepen one’s conduct of office. This is what it means to say that those holding office should understand what comes first and what comes afterward in relation to learning.
As for beginning with the extension of knowledge and ending with vigorous practice, everything concerned with cultivating oneself belongs to learning, and learning has its own tasks. One investigates things and exhaustively explores their principles to distinguish and analyze the myriad affairs; one makes one’s intentions sincere and rectifies one’s mind to seek to abide in the highest good. As though cutting and filing, carving and polishing, one still fears falling short. Would this be the time to turn to officeholding? Only when one understands categories and comprehends their connections, so that one’s analysis of the myriad affairs is precise; when one stands firm without turning back, and has attained the highest good one seeks—only then does one have energy to spare from learning. Then one occupies an official position and receives its emoluments, undertaking the ordering of the state…

也行其義達其道以發揮於事業也學優而仕
則既有以攻其學而不怠又有以驗其學而益
廣所謂學者之於仕當知所先後蓋如此然則
當其仕學而志有所分力有所奪者寧不兩失

也，行其義，達其道，以發揮於事業也。學優而仕，則既有以攻其學而不怠，又有以驗其學而益廣。所謂學者之於仕當知所先後，蓋如此。然則當其仕學，而志有所分、力有所奪者，寧不兩失之邪？大抵學者仕之體，仕者學之用。學而不仕，則其體為無用，如荷蓧丈人之流是也；仕而不學，則其用為無體，如原伯魯之不說學是也。子夏先言仕，後言學，其意蓋各有所指。要之，學先仕後，其序不可亂也。此又學者之所當知。

尊賢使能，俊傑在位，則天下之士皆悅而願立於其朝矣。
高軒

translation_en:
…and put righteousness into practice and give effect to the Way, manifesting them in practical achievements. If one takes office after attaining proficiency in learning, one can both pursue one’s studies without slackening and put one’s learning to the test, broadening it still further. This is what is meant by saying that those who study must understand what comes first and what comes afterward in relation to taking office. But if, in undertaking office and study, their purpose is divided and their energies diverted, will they not fail at both? Broadly speaking, learning is the substance underlying official service, and official service is the application of learning. To study without taking office leaves that substance without application, as with such men as the old man carrying a weeding basket. To take office without studying leaves that application without substance, as with Yuan Bolu, who took no pleasure in learning. Zixia speaks first of office and then of learning, each statement evidently addressing a particular circumstance. In essence, learning comes first and office afterward: this order must not be confused. This, too, is something students ought to understand.

“Honor the worthy and employ the capable, with outstanding men in office; then all the scholars of the realm will rejoice and wish to stand at your court.”
By Gao Xuan.

Associate Examiner Yao, Professor, comments: “This is the foremost matter in practicing kingly government, and the essay succeeds in bringing it out. Its author must be an accomplished writer; hence I have singled it out for inclusion.”

Examiner Mao, Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “The passage explaining ‘outstanding men’ is clear.”

Examiner Fu, Academician, comments: “This is indeed what Mencius meant.”

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
惟國君能用夫士故士皆樂為之臣蓋士未嘗
不欲仕也孰謂國君能用士而不可以得天下
之士之心哉贊孟子之意謂夫國家當以王政
為務而王政必以人才為先今之諸侯誠知夫
賢而有德者上下所賴則貴其德而尊尚之諫
則必行言則必聽非徒禮貌之而已誠知夫能
而有才者政事所資則量其才而任使之外憫
其勞內恤其誠非徒富貴之而已衆賢之中有
俊傑焉乃德之異者也於是拔之草茅置諸具
===
瞻之地何窮躓之有衆能之中有俊傑焉乃才
之異者也於是起於巖穴荐陟浚明之位何屈
抑之有國之能用士如此天下之士其有不應
之者乎將見自西自東各封疆也士之在彼者
聞我尚賢之聲莫不欣然而悅以為道可行時
可濟也孰不願往而立於其朝乎自南自北殊
政教也士之居彼者慕我達才之風莫不躍然
而喜以為志可得澤可加也孰不欲進而履於
其庭乎夫士也者民之先也天下之士悅而民

punctuated: 惟國君能用夫士，故士皆樂為之臣。蓋士未嘗不欲仕也，孰謂國君能用士而不可以得天下之士之心哉？贊孟子之意，謂夫國家當以王政為務，而王政必以人才為先。今之諸侯誠知夫賢而有德者上下所賴，則貴其德而尊尚之，諫則必行，言則必聽，非徒禮貌之而已。誠知夫能而有才者政事所資，則量其才而任使之，外憫其勞，內恤其誠，非徒富貴之而已。衆賢之中有俊傑焉，乃德之異者也，於是拔之草茅，置諸具瞻之地，何窮躓之有？衆能之中有俊傑焉，乃才之異者也，於是起於巖穴，荐陟浚明之位，何屈抑之有？國之能用士如此，天下之士其有不應之者乎？將見自西自東，各封疆也，士之在彼者聞我尚賢之聲，莫不欣然而悅，以為道可行，時可濟也，孰不願往而立於其朝乎？自南自北，殊政教也，士之居彼者慕我達才之風，莫不躍然而喜，以為志可得，澤可加也，孰不欲進而履於其庭乎？夫士也者，民之先也。天下之士悅而民
translation_en:
Only when the ruler of a state can employ scholars are scholars all glad to become his subjects. Scholars have never been unwilling to take office. Who could say that a ruler capable of employing scholars cannot win the hearts of scholars throughout the realm? Expounding Mengzi’s meaning, we say that a state should make kingly government its chief concern, and that kingly government must give priority to men of talent. If the feudal lords of today truly recognize that worthy men possessing virtue are those upon whom high and low alike depend, they will prize their virtue and honor them: they will invariably act upon their remonstrances and heed their words, rather than merely treating them with ceremonial courtesy. If they truly recognize that capable men possessing talent provide the resources for government, they will assess their abilities and employ them accordingly, showing concern outwardly for their toil and inwardly for their sincerity, rather than merely enriching and ennobling them.

Among the many worthy men are outstanding figures whose virtue is exceptional. If these are drawn from obscurity and placed in positions to which all look up, how could they remain impoverished and frustrated? Among the many capable men are outstanding figures whose talent is exceptional. If these are summoned from their secluded retreats among cliffs and caves, recommended, and advanced to positions for men of profound insight [?], how could they remain thwarted and suppressed? When a state employs scholars in this manner, could any scholar throughout the realm fail to respond?

Then one will see that, from west and east, though each land has its own boundaries, the scholars there, hearing of our reputation for honoring the worthy, will all rejoice. Believing that the Way can be put into practice and the troubles of the age remedied, who would not wish to go and stand at such a ruler’s court? From south and north, though government and instruction differ, the scholars dwelling there, admiring our practice of advancing talented men, will all leap with joy. Believing that their aspirations can be fulfilled and their beneficence extended to others, who would not wish to come forward and enter his court? Scholars are the leaders of the people. When the scholars throughout the realm are pleased, the people…

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
從之矣斯其於王天下也何有哉抑此特王政
之一事耳然不先務此欲王政之行得乎故孟
子將言所以救民者四事而必以是先焉蓋即
書所謂立政惟人者以人立政以政養民而民
焉有不歸者哉百里可王無敵於天下之言非
苟為大而已戰國之君徒知尊臏起貴儀秦而
才如亞聖顧使之終身不遇可勝嘆哉
易
君子以成德為行曰可見之行也
許仁

translation_en:
…follow them. What difficulty, then, would there be in ruling all under Heaven as a true king? Yet this is only one aspect of kingly government. If this is not made the first priority, however, can kingly government be put into practice? Thus, when Mencius was about to discuss four measures for rescuing the people, he necessarily placed this first. This is precisely what the Book of Documents means by “Establishing government depends upon men.” Through worthy men one establishes government, and through government one nourishes the people: how could the people fail to turn to such a ruler? The statements that “with a territory of a hundred li one can become a true king” and that one can be “without rival under Heaven” are no mere exaggerations. The rulers of the Warring States knew only to honor Sun Bin and Wu Qi and esteem Zhang Yi and Su Qin; yet they allowed a man as talented as the Second Sage, Mencius, to go his entire life without finding a ruler who would employ him. How deeply lamentable!

Book of Changes
“The gentleman takes perfected virtue as his conduct.” It is said: “This is conduct that can be seen.”
Xu Ren

Comment by Associate Examiner Hou, Instructor: On this topic, candidates generally follow Shuanghu’s interpretation, which does not accord with the Original Meaning. This essay alone offers a firm judgment of its own and is no careless composition. It is sufficient to dispel the confusion arising from entrenched habits of interpretation.

Comment by Associate Examiner Bin, Instructor: Its writing and reasoning are refined and exact; reading it makes one sit up in astonishment. The author clearly has a profound understanding of the Book of Changes. This essay should be selected to head this examining room’s submissions.

Comment by Examiner Mao, Expositor-in-waiting: Only an essay written in this way accords with the Original Meaning.

Comment by Examiner Fu, Academician: It expounds principle with fluency of expression. An excellent composition.

The Commentary on the Words of the Text discusses how the gentleman’s conduct, as it issues forth, is rooted in his own person; hence, when his conduct reaches fulfillment, it cannot be concealed. For virtue is the foundation of conduct. The gentleman takes perfected virtue as his conduct; thus …

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
宜其行之不可揜如此夫乾文言申初九之義
将言乎君子之所以弗用也而先及此且所謂
君子以成德為行者何哉誠以天下之理聚於
人心而散於萬事君子之德所以備衆理於一
貫者意既誠心既正而道之積厥躬者粹然矣
是德也豈終蘊而不發乎道與時逢則舉而措
之出乎身加乎民其施之天下國家者即其意
誠心正之事業也君子之德所以立天下之大
本者誠之至性之盡而理之根於心者渾然矣
===
是德也豈終含而不露乎位與德遇則推而行
之發乎邇見乎遠其賛乎天地化育者即其至
誠盡性之功用也君子之以成德為行也如此
又何以曰日可見之行哉盖君子之道有體有
用德其體也行其用也立其體斯達諸用故自
家齊國治而至於天下平其事業之就如火然
泉達日彰著而不已炳然蔚然豈若蘊於中者
之不可見乎君子之道有内有外德其内也行
其外也誠於中必形於外故自盡人盡物而至

其外也誠於中必形於外故自盡人盡物而至
punctuated: 宜其行之不可揜如此。夫乾文言申初九之義，将言乎君子之所以弗用也，而先及此。且所謂君子以成德為行者何哉？誠以天下之理聚於人心而散於萬事，君子之德所以備衆理於一貫者，意既誠，心既正，而道之積厥躬者粹然矣。是德也，豈終蘊而不發乎？道與時逢，則舉而措之，出乎身，加乎民，其施之天下國家者，即其意誠心正之事業也。君子之德所以立天下之大本者，誠之至，性之盡，而理之根於心者渾然矣。是德也，豈終含而不露乎？位與德遇，則推而行之，發乎邇，見乎遠，其賛乎天地化育者，即其至誠盡性之功用也。君子之以成德為行也如此，又何以曰日可見之行哉？盖君子之道有體有用，德其體也，行其用也。立其體，斯達諸用，故自家齊國治而至於天下平，其事業之就如火然泉達，日彰著而不已，炳然蔚然，豈若蘊於中者之不可見乎？君子之道有内有外，德其内也，行其外也。誠於中，必形於外，故自盡人盡物而至

…it is fitting that his conduct should be impossible to conceal in this way. The Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan) for the hexagram Qian elaborates the meaning of the initial nine. It is about to explain why the gentleman does not put himself to use, yet first touches upon this. What, then, does it mean to say that the gentleman makes perfected virtue his conduct? It is because the principles of all under Heaven gather in the human mind and extend throughout the myriad affairs. The gentleman’s virtue comprehends these many principles in a single unity: once his intentions are sincere and his mind is rectified, the Way accumulated within his person is pure. Could such virtue remain stored within forever, never finding expression? When the Way encounters its proper time, he brings it forth and puts it into practice. It proceeds from his person and reaches the people; what he applies to the realm and its states is precisely the undertaking that issues from sincere intentions and a rectified mind. The gentleman’s virtue establishes the great foundation of all under Heaven: with sincerity brought to its utmost and his nature fully realized, the principles rooted in his mind form an integral whole. Could such virtue remain contained forever, never revealing itself? When official position accords with virtue, he extends it into action. It issues forth nearby and becomes manifest far away; his assistance in the transforming and nourishing work of Heaven and Earth is precisely the efficacy of utmost sincerity and the full realization of his nature.

Such is the gentleman’s making perfected virtue his conduct. Why, then, does the text also speak of conduct that can be seen day by day? The gentleman’s Way has substance and function: virtue is its substance, and conduct its function. Once its substance is established, it finds expression in its function. Thus, from ordering the family and governing the state to bringing peace to all under Heaven, the accomplishment of his undertakings is like fire taking flame and a spring breaking forth. Day by day it becomes ever more manifest, brilliant and splendid. How could it be as invisible as something stored within? The gentleman’s Way has an inner and an outer aspect: virtue is its inner aspect, and conduct its outer aspect. What is sincere within must take form without. title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
於與天地參其功用之大如天覆地載日昭灼
而莫揜巍然煥然豈若含於中者之不可睹乎
君子之行其顯而可見也如此初之德固無不
足而其行則未可見焉此其所以弗用而有所
待歟斯義也古之人有行之者伊尹太公是也
方其耕莘野釣渭陽其行而未成之時乎及其
出而阿衡有商為周尚父成順天應人之王業
其日可見之行乎然伊尹樂堯舜之道太公天
下之大老也則其以成德為行又安可誣哉學

於與天地參，其功用之大，如天覆地載，日昭灼而莫揜，巍然煥然，豈若含於中者之不可睹乎？君子之行，其顯而可見也如此。初之德固無不足，而其行則未可見焉，此其所以弗用而有所待歟？斯義也，古之人有行之者，伊尹、太公是也。方其耕莘野、釣渭陽，其行而未成之時乎？及其出而阿衡有商、為周尚父，成順天應人之王業，其日可見之行乎？然伊尹樂堯舜之道，太公天下之大老也，則其以成德為行，又安可誣哉？學易者以是徵之，則孔子之言益信。
益，動而巽，日進无疆；天施地生，其益无方。
胡昭

translation_en:
…to standing alongside Heaven and Earth as a third power: the greatness of his efficacy is like Heaven covering and Earth bearing all things, shining forth daily with a brilliance that cannot be concealed, lofty and radiant. How could it be as invisible as what remains contained within? Such is the manifest visibility of the gentleman’s conduct. At first, his virtue certainly lacked nothing, yet his conduct could not be seen. Is this why he remained out of service, awaiting his time? Among the ancients, Yi Yin and Taigong put this principle into practice. When one ploughed the fields of Shen and the other fished on the northern bank of the Wei, was this not the time when their conduct had yet to reach fulfillment? When they emerged, one becoming chief minister to the Shang and the other the Zhou’s Venerated Father, and brought to fruition the kingly enterprise that accorded with Heaven and responded to the people, was this not their conduct becoming visible day by day? Yet Yi Yin delighted in the Way of Yao and Shun, and Taigong was the great elder of the world. How, then, could one deny that they made perfected virtue the basis of their conduct? Those who study the Book of Changes and examine this evidence will find Confucius’s words all the more trustworthy.

“Increase: movement with compliance; daily progress without limit. Heaven bestows and Earth brings forth; their increase is unrestricted.”

Hu Zhao

Comment by Associate Examiner Hou, Instructor: Movement and compliance both refer to virtues; in the Way of Increase, both should be fully realized together. Many overlook this. In treating bestowal and generation, too, they lack close appreciation. If one seeks concise expression that exhausts the meaning and sweeps away the air of stale convention, this essay must be chosen.

Comment by Associate Examiner Ning, Instructor: Among those writing in the examination hall, many lack precise understanding of movement, compliance, bestowal, and generation. This essay grasps them, and has therefore been selected for inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Mao, Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting: In explaining the greatness of Increase, the other scripts do not equal this one.

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官學士傅批是善言益者
卦德具人事之益卦體具造化之益彖傳各著
其義也盖益之道無間於人事造化者也觀於
卦德卦體可見矣昔夫子傳益之彖至此賛益
之大以為不探益卦之蘊不知益道之大以言
乎人事有如止而不動動而不巽以之進德修
業其能有益乎觀乎益之為卦下體曰震上體
曰巽震以一陽起於下動之德也巽以一陰伏
於下巽之德也以震動以巽入則是自強不息
===
===
而有極深研幾之慮勇往力行而無欲速銳進
之失學務時敏且遜志如不能治欲奮庸恒兢
業而内省由是道德之味日新事業之基日廣
士而賢賢而聖厥修乃来如川之方至也勉而
利利而安其道大光如日之方升也其為益又
安有疆限之可言哉所謂人事之益其大有如
此者以言乎造化有如天不施地不生雖曰兼
覆並載其何所益乎觀乎益之為卦上體本乾
下體本坤乾以一陽交於下天之施也坤以一

考試官學士傅批：是善言益者。

卦德具人事之益，卦體具造化之益，彖傳各著其義也。盖益之道，無間於人事造化者也，觀於卦德卦體可見矣。昔夫子傳益之彖，至此賛益之大，以為不探益卦之蘊，不知益道之大。以言乎人事，有如止而不動，動而不巽，以之進德修業，其能有益乎？觀乎益之為卦，下體曰震，上體曰巽。震以一陽起於下，動之德也；巽以一陰伏於下，巽之德也。以震動，以巽入，則是自強不息，而有極深研幾之慮；勇往力行，而無欲速銳進之失。學務時敏，且遜志如不能；治欲奮庸，恒兢業而内省。由是道德之味日新，事業之基日廣。士而賢，賢而聖，厥修乃来，如川之方至也；勉而利，利而安，其道大光，如日之方升也。其為益，又安有疆限之可言哉？所謂人事之益，其大有如此者。以言乎造化，有如天不施，地不生，雖曰兼覆並載，其何所益乎？觀乎益之為卦，上體本乾，下體本坤。乾以一陽交於下，天之施也；坤以一
translation_en:
Examiner Fu, Academician, comments: “This is someone who speaks well of Increase.”

The virtues of the hexagram embody increase in human affairs; its structure embodies increase in the creative transformations of Heaven and Earth. The Commentary on the Judgment makes clear the meaning of each. For the Way of Increase extends without distinction through human affairs and cosmic transformation, as can be seen in the hexagram’s virtues and structure. When the Master explained the Judgment of Increase, he reached this point and praised the greatness of increase, holding that without probing the deeper implications of the hexagram, one could not understand the greatness of its Way.

Speaking of human affairs: if one remains still without acting, or acts without yielding, can one thereby gain anything in advancing virtue and cultivating one’s undertakings? Consider the hexagram Increase: its lower trigram is Zhen, Thunder, and its upper trigram is Xun, Wind. In Zhen, a single yang line rises from below: this is the virtue of movement. In Xun, a single yin line lies beneath: this is the virtue of yielding. To move through Zhen and enter through Xun is to strive unceasingly for self-improvement while giving thought to plumbing the depths and examining the first stirrings of change; it is to advance courageously and act vigorously without the fault of craving quick results and rushing ahead. In learning, one strives for constant diligence while keeping one’s aspirations humble, as though one lacked ability. In governing, one seeks to exert oneself in service, remaining ever vigilant and examining oneself inwardly. Thus the savor of moral virtue grows fresh each day, and the foundations of one’s undertakings broaden daily. From scholar to worthy, from worthy to sage, the fruits of cultivation come like a river’s advancing flow. From strenuous effort to ready practice, from ready practice to effortless ease, one’s Way shines brightly like the rising sun. How could such increase have any bounds? Such is the greatness of what is called increase in human affairs.

Speaking of cosmic transformation: if Heaven did not bestow and Earth did not bring forth, then even though they were said to cover and sustain all things, what benefit would they confer? Consider the hexagram Increase: its upper trigram was originally Qian, Heaven, and its lower trigram was originally Kun, Earth. text:
陰達於上地之生也天布施地發生則是乾元
資始而承以坤元資生之德天道下降而應以
地道上行之功易知簡能本健順而發育見象
形器合陰陽而成化由是生物之多不測六合
之内皆春顯諸仁藏諸用盛德大業一至神之
所為也出乎震成乎艮四時萬物一帝之功用
也其為益又安有方所之可求哉所謂造化之
益其大有如此者夫子以卦德卦體而極言之
厥㫖微矣大抵易之為書廣大悉備周子所謂

陰達於上，地之生也。天布施，地發生，則是乾元資始，而承以坤元資生之德；天道下降，而應以地道上行之功。易知簡能，本健順而發育；見象形器，合陰陽而成化。由是生物之多不測，六合之内皆春。顯諸仁，藏諸用，盛德大業，一至神之所為也；出乎震，成乎艮，四時萬物，一帝之功用也。其為益，又安有方所之可求哉？所謂造化之益，其大有如此者。夫子以卦德卦體而極言之，厥㫖微矣。大抵《易》之為書，廣大悉備，周子所謂精以畫示，蘊因卦發，而五經之源、天地鬼神之奥者也。然一言以蔽之，曰時而已。益之時，在人事，則動巽之德，雖聖人不能違；在造化，則施生之益，雖天地不能違，皆所以趣乎時也。故夫子又曰：「凡益之道，與時偕行。」大哉，時乎！知此者，可與言《易》矣。

translation_en:
…a yin line reaches upward: this is Earth's generation. Heaven bestows and Earth brings forth life. Thus Qian's primal power, from which things receive their beginnings, is sustained by the virtue of Kun's primal power, from which things receive life; the downward movement of Heaven's way is answered by the achievement of Earth's way moving upward. Knowing through ease and acting through simplicity, they nurture growth on the basis of vigor and compliance; manifesting images and giving shape to concrete things, they unite yin and yang to accomplish transformation. Thus the multitude of living things they produce is beyond reckoning, and spring fills all six directions. Manifest in benevolence and concealed in its workings, their abundant virtue and great enterprise are entirely the work of the utmost spiritual potency. Coming forth in Zhen and reaching completion in Gen, the four seasons and myriad things are entirely the workings of the Lord on High. How could such increase be sought within any fixed spatial bounds? Such is the greatness of what is called the increase bestowed by creation and transformation. The Master expounded it fully through the hexagram's virtues and structure; his meaning is subtle indeed.

Broadly speaking, the Book of Changes is vast and all-encompassing. As Master Zhou said, its essential meaning is shown through the lines, and its hidden depths unfold through the hexagrams; it is the source of the Five Classics and holds the mysteries of Heaven, Earth, ghosts, and spirits. Yet one word sums it up: timeliness. In the time of Increase, as regards human affairs, even the sage cannot depart from the virtues of movement and compliance; as regards creation and transformation, even Heaven and Earth cannot depart from the increase wrought by bestowal and generation. All of these accord with the time. Thus the Master also said: “Every way of bringing increase proceeds in step with the time.” Great indeed is timeliness! With one who understands this, it is possible to discuss the Book of Changes.

Book of Documents

text:
克邁乃訓
頓銳
同考試官教諭陳批訓志成德九峰傳意士子
率多遺漏此篇摹寫獨真故錄之
同考試官教授姚批此篇求訓克邁處體認親
切且能組織傳註成文盖嘗究心於經學者
考試官侍講學士毛批順題說去而當時語意淺深
自見正不必騁奇耳
考試官學士傅批正說出高宗責望傅說之意
===
賢王命大臣以輔德必喻以資之切而示以行
之力也盖君德之所繫大矣在人者資之切而
在己者行之力賢王之望於大臣也何深哉昔
高宗命傅說之意謂夫德必由學而進學必以
志為先予誠願進於德也而知則未至爾其時
發德音以訓我使志不昧於所趨予誠有意於
學也而志則未通爾其開陳善道以誨我俾心
不眩於所事是何也君德之修必賴賢人之助
譬之為酒醴而需麴糵爾非我之麴糵乎君德

賢王命大臣以輔德必喻以資之切而示以行
之力也蓋君德之所繫大矣在人者資之切而
在己者行之力賢王之望於大臣也何深哉昔
高宗命傅說之意謂夫德必由學而進學必以
志為先予誠願進於德也而知則未至爾其時
發德音以訓我使志不昧於所趨予誠有意於
學也而志則未通爾其開陳善道以誨我俾心
不眩於所事是何也君德之修必須賢人之助
譬之為酒醴而需麴蘖爾非我之麴蘖乎君德
punctuated:
克邁乃訓。
頓銳。

同考試官教授姚批：此篇求訓克邁處，體認親切，且能組織傳註成文，盖嘗究心於經學者。

賢王命大臣以輔德，必喻以資之切，而示以行之力也。盖君德之所繫大矣，在人者資之切，而在己者行之力。賢王之望於大臣也，何深哉！昔高宗命傅說之意，謂夫德必由學而進，學必以志為先。予誠願進於德也，而知則未至，爾其時發德音以訓我，使志不昧於所趨。予誠有意於學也，而志則未通，爾其開陳善道以誨我，俾心不眩於所事。是何也？君德之修，必賴賢人之助。譬之為酒醴而需麴糵，爾非我之麴糵乎？君德
translation_en:
…be able to carry out your instructions.

Dun Rui.

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, School Instructor: Guiding the ruler’s intentions and perfecting his virtue—this is the meaning of Jiufeng’s commentary, which candidates generally overlook. This essay alone conveys it faithfully; hence its inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yao, School Instructor: This essay shows an intimate understanding of the passages concerning seeking instruction and being able to carry it out. Moreover, it weaves the commentaries and annotations into a coherent composition. Its author has evidently devoted himself to the study of the Classics.

Comment by Examiner Mao, Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting: The exposition follows the topic, and the various depths of meaning in the original utterance become apparent of themselves. There is certainly no need to strive for novelty.

Comment by Examiner Fu, Academician: This precisely expresses what Gaozong expected and demanded of Fu Yue.

When a worthy king commands a great minister to assist him in cultivating virtue, he must illustrate how urgently he needs that assistance and declare how vigorously he will put the instruction into practice. For much depends upon the ruler’s virtue. What rests with others is the indispensable assistance they provide; what rests with himself is strenuous practice. How profound are a worthy king’s expectations of his great ministers!

The meaning of Gaozong’s command to Fu Yue in former times was this: “Virtue must advance through learning, and learning must begin with the resolve to learn. I sincerely wish to advance in virtue, but my understanding has not yet attained its goal. You should offer virtuous counsel at the proper times to instruct me, so that my resolve is not ignorant of the direction it should take. I sincerely intend to learn, but my purpose is not yet fully clear. You should expound the good Way to teach me, so that my mind is not confused about what it should pursue. Why is this? The cultivation of a ruler’s virtue necessarily depends upon the assistance of worthy men. It is like making wine and sweet wine, which requires yeast cakes and malted grain: are you not my yeast cakes and malted grain? The ruler’s virtue…”

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之成必藉正人之力譬之作和羹而用鹽梅爾
非我之鹽梅乎麴糵之為酒也在甘苦得中而
爾於我之性行不思所以交修之可乎盖必以
柔濟剛左右規正以成其德其毋我棄曰是不
可與有言也鹽梅之作羹也貴酸鹹適均而爾
於我之身心不圖所以交修之可乎盖必以可
濟否朝夕匡救以勸其學其勿予舍曰是不足
與有為也夫知之而不能蹈是自棄其德矣故
我於爾之訓入乎耳則必存乎心豈患予之不
===
能邪聞之而不克行是自廢其學矣故我於爾
之誨誦於口則必體諸身何憂予之不克邪高
宗命傅說如此則其篤志於學者可知而德之
成也不難矣抑論之自古帝王莫不有師若湯
之於伊尹學焉而後臣之是已高宗得傅說置
之師保之位其說命三篇君臣之所留意者惟
輔德進學之事求之篤應之誠可謂上下交而
其志同矣其視烈祖阿衡之相遇殆無以異商
道之復興也宜哉

道之復興也宜哉
punctuated:
之成，必藉正人之力。譬之作和羹而用鹽梅，爾非我之鹽梅乎？麴糵之為酒也，在甘苦得中，而爾於我之性行，不思所以交修之可乎？盖必以柔濟剛，左右規正，以成其德。其毋我棄，曰：「是不可與有言也。」鹽梅之作羹也，貴酸鹹適均，而爾於我之身心，不圖所以交修之可乎？盖必以可濟否，朝夕匡救，以勸其學。其勿予舍，曰：「是不足與有為也。」夫知之而不能蹈，是自棄其德矣。故我於爾之訓，入乎耳則必存乎心，豈患予之不能邪？聞之而不克行，是自廢其學矣。故我於爾之誨，誦於口則必體諸身，何憂予之不克邪？高宗命傅說如此，則其篤志於學者可知，而德之成也不難矣。
抑論之，自古帝王莫不有師，若湯之於伊尹，學焉而後臣之，是已。高宗得傅說，置之師保之位，其說命三篇，君臣之所留意者，惟輔德進學之事。求之篤，應之誠，可謂上下交而其志同矣。其視烈祖阿衡之相遇，殆無以異。商道之復興也，宜哉！
translation_en:
…the perfection of the ruler’s virtue must depend upon the efforts of upright men. It is like making a well-seasoned broth with salt and sour plums: are you not my salt and plums? When ferment is used to make wine, the sweetness and bitterness must be properly balanced. Can you, then, fail to consider how to cultivate and correct my disposition and conduct in every respect? You must temper firmness with gentleness, guiding and correcting me on every side to perfect my virtue. Do not abandon me, saying, ‘This is someone with whom one cannot discuss anything.’ When salt and plums are used to make broth, what matters is a proper balance of sourness and saltiness. Can you, then, fail to plan how to cultivate and correct my person and mind in every respect? You must remedy what is wrong with what is right, correcting my faults morning and evening to encourage my learning. Do not forsake me, saying, ‘This is someone with whom nothing can be accomplished.’ To know something yet be unable to put it into practice is to abandon one’s own virtue. Thus, when your instructions enter my ears, I will certainly preserve them in my heart. Why fear that I will be unable to do so? To hear something yet fail to act upon it is to cast aside one’s own learning. Thus, when I recite your teachings with my mouth, I will certainly embody them in my conduct. Why worry that I will fail? Such were Gaozong’s charges to Fu Yue. From them we can see how firmly he set his will upon learning; the perfection of his virtue was therefore no difficult matter.
Furthermore, from antiquity emperors and kings have all had teachers. Tang’s relationship with Yi Yin is an example: he learned from him before making him his minister. When Gaozong obtained Fu Yue’s services, he placed him in the position of preceptor and guardian. In the three chapters of the Charge to Yue, the ruler and minister devoted their attention solely to assisting the cultivation of virtue and advancing learning. The ruler sought instruction earnestly, and the minister responded sincerely. It may indeed be said that superior and subordinate communicated with one another and shared a common purpose. Compared with the meeting of the illustrious ancestor Tang and his chief minister Yi Yin, this was scarcely different. How fitting that the way of Shang should flourish again!

初一曰五行次二曰敬用五事
呂𢘆

精處此作辭足達意讀之自覺有味取之
考試官侍講學士毛批五行五事該括洪範一篇
之意觀此作可知矣
考試官學士傅批聖人叙疇之意發揮殆盡
===
聖人於洛書一二之數有第以天道者有第以
人事者蓋五行在天而五事在人者也聖人叙
疇其孰先於此哉箕子陳洪範先舉九疇之綱
而此其二也吾想夫洪水告平洛龜呈瑞竒偶
之數始分天人之理莫辨禹也心會神領而數
既明繼天立極而疇以序彼其位居坎而間於
六八者非一乎一者水之生氣之始也盖一畫
之數莫先焉故曰初禹以為天之道惟五行為
大是宜序九疇之首矣乃於一而第之以五行

聖人於洛書一二之數，有第以天道者，有第以人事者，蓋五行在天而五事在人者也。聖人叙疇，其孰先於此哉？箕子陳洪範，先舉九疇之綱，而此其二也。吾想夫洪水告平，洛龜呈瑞，竒偶之數始分，天人之理莫辨。禹也心會神領，而數既明；繼天立極，而疇以序。彼其位居坎而間於六八者，非一乎？一者，水之生，氣之始也。盖一畫之數莫先焉，故曰初。禹以為天之道惟五行為大，是宜序九疇之首矣，乃於一而第之以五行
translation_en:
“First comes the Five Phases; second comes the reverent application of the Five Activities.”
Lü Heng 呂𢘆
Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor, comments: “The relationship between Heaven and humanity is exceedingly difficult to discuss. This essay succeeds in discussing it: its author is surely a scholar who has attained an understanding of principle.”
Associate Examiner Yao, Professor, comments: “Essays on the Great Plan generally find it difficult to reach its subtleties. In this essay, the language adequately conveys the meaning, and reading it, one naturally finds it rewarding. Accept it.”
Examiner Mao, Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “The Five Phases and the Five Activities encompass the meaning of the entire Great Plan chapter. Reading this essay makes that clear.”
Examiner Fu, Academician, comments: “The sage’s intention in arranging the categories has been expounded almost exhaustively.”
In assigning categories to the numbers one and two of the Luo Writing, the sage assigned one to the Way of Heaven and the other to human affairs. For the Five Phases belong to Heaven, while the Five Activities belong to humanity. When the sage arranged the categories, what could have taken precedence over these? When Jizi expounded the Great Plan, he first set forth the outline of its nine categories, and these are two of them. I imagine that when the great flood had been quelled and the tortoise of the Luo River displayed its auspicious markings, the odd and even numbers had only just been distinguished, while the principles of Heaven and humanity remained undiscriminated. Yu apprehended them in his heart and grasped them in spirit, and thus the numbers became clear; following Heaven, he established the ultimate standard, and thus the categories were put in order. Is not the number occupying the position of Kan, between six and eight, the number one? One is the generating number of water and the beginning of vital energy. No number precedes that of a single stroke; hence the text says “first.” Yu considered the Five Phases paramount in the Way of Heaven, so they ought to be placed at the head of the nine categories. Accordingly, to the number one he assigned the Five Phases…

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
焉五行者天之所生以養乎人者也其氣運於
天而不息其材用於世而不匱微而太極之妙
具於此顯而變化之迹成於此人君治天下之
道有經有權其用雖廣何者非五行之理為之
用邪五行之所以第於初一者蓋如此乃若位
居坤而間於七九者非二乎二者火之生氣之
著也蓋四偶之數莫先焉故曰次禹以為人之
道惟五事為切是宜序五行之次矣乃於二而
第之以敬用五事焉五事者天之所賦而具於
===
人者也以之治心必敬戒而弗怠以之修身必
祗畏而弗肆內而本然之性有以盡外而當然
之則無所違人君制天下之事有常有變其道
雖大何者非五事之敬為之本邪五事之所以
第於次二者蓋如此是則由五行而及五事以
五事而參五行天未始不為人而人亦未始不
為天也天人之理合一而無間如此非聖人其
孰能知之抑論人君治天下之法未有出於九
疇者然本諸天道固以五行為先要諸人事又

translation_en: …in that position. The Five Phases are what Heaven generates to nourish humankind. Their vital energies circulate through Heaven without ceasing, and their material resources serve the world without exhaustion. In their subtle aspect, the mysteries of the Supreme Ultimate are fully present in them; in their manifest aspect, the traces of transformation take shape in them. The ruler’s way of governing all under Heaven includes both constant principles and discretionary responses. Though its applications are extensive, which of them does not put the principles of the Five Phases to use? This, broadly speaking, is why the Five Phases are ranked under “First, one.” As for that which occupies the position of Kun and lies between seven and nine, is this not two? Two is the generating number of fire and the manifestation of vital energy. Among the four even numbers, none precedes it; hence the wording “Next.” Yu considered the Five Activities the most pressing concern in the human way, and thus fittingly placed them immediately after the Five Phases. Accordingly, under two he ranked “the reverent use of the Five Activities.” The Five Activities are what Heaven endows and human beings possess. In using them to govern the mind, one must be reverent and watchful, never negligent; in using them to cultivate oneself, one must be respectful and apprehensive, never unrestrained. Inwardly, one thereby fully realizes one’s original nature; outwardly, one violates none of the standards of what is right. The ruler’s management of the affairs of all under Heaven involves both regular circumstances and changes. Though his way is vast, what part of it does not take reverence in the Five Activities as its foundation? This, broadly speaking, is why the Five Activities are ranked under “Next, two.” Thus one proceeds from the Five Phases to the Five Activities, and through the Five Activities participates in the Five Phases. Heaven never ceases to act for humankind, and humankind likewise never ceases to act for Heaven. The principles of Heaven and humankind are united as one, without any separation, in this manner. Who but a sage could understand this? Moreover, concerning the ruler’s methods of governing all under Heaven, none falls outside the Nine Categories. Yet, when grounding them in the Way of Heaven, one certainly gives precedence to the Five Phases; when considering what is essential in human affairs, one also…

text:

translation_en:
…takes the Five Affairs as the urgent priority. Thus, when the Great Yu reached this point in arranging the categories, he spoke specifically of their reverent application. His intention can be understood. Commentators say that reverence is prescribed for the Five Affairs as the means of making oneself sincere. Through reverence—reverence that makes oneself sincere—the substance and functioning of the August Ultimate can be united by a single principle, leaving nothing out. How could this be neglected or treated without care?

The Book of Odes

“How graceful, how lovely! His hair is bound in two hornlike tufts. Before long, we see him again: suddenly he wears an adult’s cap.”

Jia Qi

Associate Examiner Zheng, Assistant Instructor, comments: This composition portrays the poet’s intention to admonish and encourage his contemporaries so vividly that it appears before our eyes. Its author must be skilled at interpreting the Odes. Accept it.

Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor, comments: Combining the commentaries into a coherent composition, this essay grasps the topic’s meaning profoundly. It is an excellent exposition of the Odes. How could its inclusion as a model be undeserved?

Associate Examiner Zhang, Professor, comments: The topic originally emerged through “陳誓揖書” [?]; from the outset, no selection was made on grounds of difficulty or ease. Of the more than one thousand scripts in my examining section, many were stymied by this topic. Late in the process I obtained this essay, excellent in both expression and reasoning, and therefore included it as a model for later students.

Examiner Mao, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: Its language is unforced yet rich in flavor. Reading it can also stir the mind.

Examiner Fu, Academician, comments: In sympathetically conveying the poet’s intention to enlighten and admonish [?] his contemporaries, one could do no better than this.

The poet uses a boy’s sudden attainment of adulthood to illustrate that the principles governing affairs require adherence to a fixed sequence…

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
蓋事理有一定之序能循其序則其極未嘗不
可至也詩人即喻以明之其意深矣昔甫田詩
人戒時人之意若謂天下之事理莫不各有其
極亦莫不各有其序躐等而求者無可達之理
循序而進者有必至之勢獨不觀諸童子乎婉
孌其弱尚未頎而長也變變其美何其娟且好
也總其角於首丱然雙出之可觀垂其餘於前
髧彼兩髦之可愛亦既見止曾幾何時矣而加
冠巍峩已突然而高聳亦既覯止曾未幾時矣
===
而載弁俅俅已忽然而高出去童子之態而並
列於成人之行謝幼者之儀而隨行於冠者之
次若是者非其躐等而强求之也盖循其少長
之序勢有所必至耳然詩人豈徒為童子評哉
正以事理之在天下也其大者皆始於其小其
遠者皆始於其近但人厭小而務大則欲速之
心萌而大反不可至矣忽近而圖遠則見利之
意作而遠終不可及矣誠能盈科而進先小而
後大則大者可一朝而得成章而達由近以及

punctuated: 蓋事理有一定之序，能循其序，則其極未嘗不可至也。詩人即喻以明之，其意深矣。昔甫田詩人戒時人之意，若謂天下之事理莫不各有其極，亦莫不各有其序。躐等而求者，無可達之理；循序而進者，有必至之勢。獨不觀諸童子乎？婉孌其弱，尚未頎而長也；變變其美，何其娟且好也！總其角於首，丱然雙出之可觀；垂其餘於前，髧彼兩髦之可愛。亦既見止，曾幾何時矣，而加冠巍峩，已突然而高聳；亦既覯止，曾未幾時矣，而載弁俅俅，已忽然而高出。去童子之態，而並列於成人之行；謝幼者之儀，而隨行於冠者之次。若是者，非其躐等而强求之也，盖循其少長之序，勢有所必至耳。然詩人豈徒為童子評哉？正以事理之在天下也，其大者皆始於其小，其遠者皆始於其近。但人厭小而務大，則欲速之心萌，而大反不可至矣；忽近而圖遠，則見利之意作，而遠終不可及矣。誠能盈科而進，先小而後大，則大者可一朝而得；成章而達，由近以及
translation_en:
The affairs of the world and their underlying principles have a fixed sequence. If one can follow that sequence, their ultimate attainment is never beyond reach. The poet makes this clear through an analogy, and his meaning is profound. The admonition that the poet of “Vast Fields” (Futian) addressed to his contemporaries was as if to say: all affairs and principles under Heaven have their respective ultimate attainments, and all have their respective sequences. Those who seek to skip stages have no way of arriving; those who advance in due order are bound to reach their goal. Have you not observed a young boy? Tender and delicate in his youth, he is not yet tall and grown; with his changing beauty [?], how graceful and handsome he is! His hair is gathered into two knots atop his head, an appealing sight as they project like horns; the remaining locks hang in front, those two drooping tresses so endearing. You have seen him—and how much time has passed? Now, wearing a lofty cap, he suddenly towers tall. You have met him—and scarcely any time has passed! Now, wearing his ceremonial cap with a deferential bearing, he has suddenly grown tall. He leaves behind his boyish manner and stands among adults; he relinquishes the deportment of childhood and takes his place among capped men. This does not happen because he skips stages and forces his growth. He merely follows the sequence from youth to maturity, and the natural course necessarily brings him there.

But was the poet merely commenting on a boy? His point was precisely that, among the affairs and principles of the world, what is great always begins with what is small, and what is distant always begins with what is near. Yet when people disdain the small and strive for the great, a desire for haste arises, and greatness instead becomes unattainable. When they disregard the near and scheme for the distant, the impulse to seize advantage arises, and the distant ultimately remains beyond reach. If one can truly advance only after filling each hollow, attending first to the small and then to the great, greatness may one day be attained; if one proceeds only after completing each stage, working from what is near toward …

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
遠則遠者可一旦而致自灑掃應對而漸收乎
修齊治平之功自温恭簡諒而馴致乎美大聖
神之域若是者亦非其率意而妄為之也盖循
其先後之次理有所必然耳是則童子忽至於
成人之地人所共覩者也循序可造於事理之
極人所未諭者也詩人即彼以喻此其示人之
意何其切歟抑此詩序以為為齊襄公而作然
考其一篇之中立辭命意若無與於襄公者似
專為時人躐等之弊而發故朱子以為未見為
===
襄公之詩者得之矣噫齊以急功利喜夸詐為
俗詩人之言豈為一人道哉說詩者以意逆之
可也
左之左之君子宜之右之右之君子有之
維其有之是以似之
玉江

遠，則遠者可一旦而致。自灑掃應對而漸收乎修齊治平之功，自温恭簡諒而馴致乎美大聖神之域。若是者，亦非其率意而妄為之也，盖循其先後之次，理有所必然耳。是則童子忽至於成人之地，人所共覩者也；循序可造於事理之極，人所未諭者也。詩人即彼以喻此，其示人之意何其切歟！抑此詩序以為為齊襄公而作，然考其一篇之中，立辭命意，若無與於襄公者，似專為時人躐等之弊而發，故朱子以為未見為襄公之詩者，得之矣。噫！齊以急功利、喜夸詐為俗，詩人之言豈為一人道哉？說詩者以意逆之可也。

左之左之，君子宜之；右之右之，君子有之。維其有之，是以似之。

玉江

同考試官訓導鄭批：傳意雖明，而作者頗難措詞。此篇能於筆路窘處，從容數語，便快人意，故錄之以式後學。
translation_en:
…the distant, then what is distant can be reached in a single day. Beginning with sweeping, cleaning, and responding properly to others, one gradually achieves the work of cultivating oneself, ordering the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world. Beginning with warmth, respectfulness, simplicity, and trustworthiness, one advances by degrees to the realms of beauty, greatness, sagehood, and spiritual perfection. Such achievement likewise does not come from acting recklessly on impulse. It simply follows the proper sequence of what comes first and what comes afterward, with results that necessarily follow from principle. Thus, a boy’s suddenly reaching the standing of an adult is something everyone sees; that orderly progress can lead to the utmost realization of the principles of affairs is something people have yet to understand. The poet uses the former to explain the latter: how earnest is his intention to instruct others!

The preface to this poem, however, says that it was composed about Duke Xiang of Qi. Yet, examining the wording and intent of the entire poem, one finds apparently nothing concerning Duke Xiang. It seems directed exclusively against the contemporary fault of skipping stages. Thus Master Zhu was right to say that he could not see how this was a poem about Duke Xiang. Alas! In Qi, the prevailing customs were to pursue immediate advantage and delight in boastfulness and deceit. Could the poet’s words have been addressed to just one person? Those who interpret the Poetry may properly use their own understanding to apprehend his intention.

“On the left, on the left, the noble man is suited to it;
on the right, on the right, the noble man has the requisite qualities.
Because he possesses these,
he can carry on his forebears’ work.”

Yu Jiang

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Assistant Instructor: “Although the meaning of the commentary is clear, a writer finds it quite difficult to frame his words. Where the course of composition becomes constrained, this essay supplies a few unhurried phrases that immediately satisfy the reader. I have therefore recorded it as a model for later students.”

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭吳批平平寫出周天子稱美諸
侯之意千百載之下若親際而見之者予於吾子乎敬羡
同考試官教授張批場中作此題者率多病於枯
澁而子能易易言之殊有意味必學詩而有得於言意之表者
考試官侍講學士毛批形容似之甚好
考試官學士傅批讀此可以想見有周君臣相
與氣象
王者美君子有以周於用原君子所以周於用
盖著於外者必本諸內也孰謂君子用周於外
===
而不本於才德之有諸內者哉此天子美諸侯
之辭盖以答瞻彼洛矣也若謂人之優於德者
或短於才而我君子則才德之兼全長於才者
或歉於德而我君子則才德之咸備但見以左
之而左之無所不宜或入而立於朝也則輔理
之功宜於朝或出而處於國也則承化之功宜
於國施之當其可措之惟其時所謂宜民宜人
者是已以右之而右之無所不有或責之以文
事也則文足以附衆或責之以武事也則武足

考試官學士傅批：讀此可以想見有周君臣相與氣象。

王者美君子有以周於用，原君子所以周於用，盖著於外者必本諸內也。孰謂君子用周於外，而不本於才德之有諸內者哉？此天子美諸侯之辭，盖以答《瞻彼洛矣》也。若謂人之優於德者，或短於才，而我君子則才德之兼全；長於才者，或歉於德，而我君子則才德之咸備。但見以左之而左之，無所不宜：或入而立於朝也，則輔理之功宜於朝；或出而處於國也，則承化之功宜於國。施之當其可，措之惟其時，所謂「宜民宜人」者是已。以右之而右之，無所不有：或責之以文事也，則文足以附衆；或責之以武事也，則武足
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor, comments: In straightforward language, this conveys the Zhou Son of Heaven’s intent in praising the feudal lords. Though separated from them by hundreds and thousands of years, one feels as though personally present and witnessing them. I hold you in esteem and admiration.

Associate Examiner Zhang, Prefectural School Instructor, comments: Most candidates who treated this topic in the examination suffered from dry and labored expression. Yet you express it with ease and considerable depth of meaning. Surely you have studied the Odes and grasped something beyond their words and overt meaning.

Examiner Mao, Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: The depiction of “resembling it” is excellent.

Examiner Fu, Academician, comments: Reading this, one can picture the spirit of mutual dealings between the ruler and ministers of Zhou.

The king praises the noble man for possessing what enables him to meet every demand of service. To trace how the noble man can meet every such demand is to recognize that what manifests itself outwardly must be rooted within. Who could say that the noble man’s comprehensive effectiveness in outward affairs is not rooted in the talent and virtue he possesses within? These are the Son of Heaven’s words praising the feudal lords, apparently in reply to the ode “Gaze upon the Luo River” (Zhan bi Luo yi). It is as though he were saying: Those who excel in virtue may be deficient in talent, but our noble man possesses both talent and virtue in full; those who excel in talent may be wanting in virtue, but our noble man is fully endowed with both. We see only that, when directed to the left, he goes to the left, and nowhere is he unsuited. If he enters and takes his place at court, his service in assisting government is fitting for the court; if he goes out and resides in his domain, his service in receiving and carrying forward the ruler’s transforming influence is fitting for that domain. He acts as circumstances require and takes measures at the proper time. This is what is meant by “suited to the common people and suited to those in office.” When directed to the right, he goes to the right, and there is nothing he lacks. If charged with civil affairs, his civil accomplishments suffice to win the allegiance of the multitude; if charged with military affairs, his martial accomplishments suffice …

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以威敵取之而不窮用之而不竭所謂有猷有
為者是已然此豈矯飾而為之邪盖其才之出
於帝降者充積於中恢恢乎其有餘地德之根
於天賦者渾融於内綽綽乎其有餘裕是以形
之於其外不獨宜於左而又有於右内外相符
如水之有源而其出無窮也豈無體之用哉見
之於其事不獨有於右而又宜於左表裏如一
若有物在中而其緒外見也豈無本之行哉是
則諸侯以是而見知於天子天子以是而稱譽
===
乎諸侯辭氣雍容情意深至自非有周之盛何
以及此抑考瞻彼洛矣諸侯所以美天子也此
詩則天子所以美諸侯也下之美上則屢願其
保家室而不以為瀆上之美下則盛稱其有才
德而不以為嫵於乎有周盛時所以君臣上下
共成正大光明之業者良有以也故孔子録詩
既録瞻彼洛矣於前即録此詩於後非無謂也
後之讀者庸可不察
春秋
