translation_en:
Mencius said: “Yu’s control of the waters followed the way of water.” Later generations need only follow this standard in dealing with flooding. When Marquis Zhao of Han built a lofty gateway, Qu Yijiu described it as “straitened times and an excessive undertaking [?],” criticizing him for failing to respond to the drought by relieving the people’s urgent distress. If so, when undertaking works to control flooding, can one act without considering the timing?

You, sir, seeing the Yellow River shift its course in the Central Plain and waters overflow in Jiangnan, wish to apply the ancients’ policies to remedy these troubles. You truly have a heart concerned for all under Heaven. In my humble view, however, even when good methods exist, if the proper time to implement them has not arrived, how could one dare employ them lightly?

Consider the Tribute of Yu: “He guided the Yellow River from Jishi as far as Dalu; it divided into the Nine Rivers, which joined to form the Ni River.” Thus, all the means by which Yu controlled the waters of the northwest accorded with water’s natural tendency to moisten and flow downward. “The Three Rivers had entered their channels, and Zhenze was settled. They floated along the Yangzi and the sea, reaching the Huai and Si.” The means by which Yu controlled the waters of the southeast likewise accorded with water’s natural tendency to moisten and flow downward.

At the beginning of the Western Han, the Nine Rivers had silted up, narrowing the great river’s passage to the sea, so that its upper reaches frequently breached their banks. Later, the river entered Qiancheng, while its channels in De and Di divided again into eight branches. The multiplicity of its outlets happened to match the ancient arrangement, and consequently the river caused no calamities for more than a thousand years. Such was the argument of Yu Que of the Yuan dynasty.

In the time of Wuyue, agricultural lands were managed and soldiers assigned to them. Work on clearing river channels and building dikes was diligently pursued, and harvests were abundant in most years. Later, when the Song dynasty unified the realm, if the harvest in Jiangnan failed, supplies were obtained from Zheyou; if Zheyou …

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
不稔則取之淮南慢於農政不復修舉由
是圩田河塘隳廢失利宋范仲淹之言如
此然則今日之患其可盡委之氣數而不
務修人事乎第在慎之而已漢賈讓言治
河有三策徙冀州之民當水衝者决黎陽
遮害亭放河使北入海上策也多穿漕渠
於冀州地使民得以溉田分殺水怒中策
也繕完故隄增卑倍薄勞費無已數逢其
害下策也王莽時關並言秦漢以来河决
===

曹衛之域其南北不過百八十里可空此
地勿以為官亭民室韓牧以為宜略於禹

punctuated: 不稔，則取之淮南，慢於農政，不復修舉，由是圩田河塘隳廢失利。宋范仲淹之言如此。然則今日之患，其可盡委之氣數而不務修人事乎？第在慎之而已。漢賈讓言治河有三策：徙冀州之民當水衝者，决黎陽遮害亭，放河使北入海，上策也；多穿漕渠於冀州地，使民得以溉田，分殺水怒，中策也；繕完故隄，增卑倍薄，勞費無已，數逢其害，下策也。王莽時關並言，秦漢以来，河决曹衛之域，其南北不過百八十里，可空此地，勿以為官亭民室。韓牧以為宜略於禹貢九河處穿為四五，當有益。凡此數策，大同小異，要皆遵大禹之法而為之者。今决溢之患不殊於昔，而漕渠之利必資於河，有能以其策酌而用之，國之利亦民之利也。宋郟亶言蘇州水利，欲順地形高下之宜，求古人蓄泄之跡，高其隄防，大其溝洫，曲者使直，狹者使廣。單鍔
translation_en:
…if the harvest there failed, supplies were obtained from Huainan. Agricultural administration was neglected, and its works were no longer repaired or maintained. Consequently, the embanked fields, rivers, and ponds fell into disrepair and ceased to yield their benefits. Such were the words of Fan Zhongyan of the Song. Can the troubles of today, then, be attributed entirely to the cycles of fate, without striving to put human affairs in order? It is simply a matter of proceeding with care.

Jia Rang of the Han said that there were three strategies for controlling the Yellow River. Moving those inhabitants of Jizhou who lay directly in the path of its current, breaching the embankment at Zhehai Pavilion in Liyang, and releasing the river to flow northward into the sea was the best strategy. Digging numerous transport canals in Jizhou, enabling the people to irrigate their fields and dividing the flow to diminish the river’s fury, was the middle strategy. Repairing the old embankments, raising the low sections and doubling the thickness of the thin ones, with endless labor and expense and repeated exposure to disaster, was the lowest strategy.

In Wang Mang’s time, Guan Bing said that, since the Qin and Han, the river’s breaches had occurred within the region of Cao and Wei, across a north–south span of no more than 180 li. This land could be vacated, with neither government stations nor private dwellings established there. Han Mu thought it would be beneficial to excavate four or five channels approximately where the nine rivers described in the Tribute of Yu had been. These strategies differ in minor respects but are broadly alike: essentially, all follow the methods of Yu the Great.

Today, the danger of breaches and flooding is no different from that of former times, while the benefits of the transport canals necessarily depend upon the Yellow River. If someone could weigh these strategies and put them into practice, the benefit to the state would also be a benefit to the people.

Jia Dan of the Song, discussing water management in Suzhou, proposed following the lie of the land as appropriate to its elevations and depressions, seeking out the traces of the ancients’ works for storing and releasing water, raising embankments, enlarging channels and ditches, straightening those that were winding, and widening those that were narrow. title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
吳中水利書欲先開吳松江尾遷沙上之
民疏吳江岸為千橋仍於下流開白蜆安
亭二江使太湖水由青龍入海趙霖上平
江水利策一曰開置港浦二曰置閘啓閉
三曰築隄裹田凡此數說或詳或略要皆
祖大禹之意而論之者今低下之田常有
水患而高仰之田每有旱災有能用其說
推而行之民之富固
國之富也雖然二簋有時易言於損弛力之
===
===
惠荒政所先示財用之當節而人窮不可
以不之恤也傅說之告高宗曰慮善以動
動惟厥時顧茲饑饉荐臻元元憔悴公私
事力率皆不足當是時而欲修治水之上
策立不世之奇功聚大衆興大役勞民耗
國困弊立見曾謂智者而為之乎然則今
日之計何居相地勢謹隄防使河入漕渠
而已矣依故道去淤澱使水有蓄洩而已
矣此則漢宋諸人謂之下策者然役小費

punctuated:
《吳中水利書》欲先開吳松江尾，遷沙上之民，疏吳江岸為千橋，仍於下流開白蜆、安亭二江，使太湖水由青龍入海。趙霖上平江水利策：一曰開置港浦，二曰置閘啓閉，三曰築隄裹田。凡此數說，或詳或略，要皆祖大禹之意而論之者。今低下之田常有水患，而高仰之田每有旱災，有能用其說推而行之，民之富固國之富也。

雖然，二簋有時，《易》言於損；弛力之惠，荒政所先。示財用之當節，而人窮不可以不之恤也。傅說之告高宗曰：「慮善以動，動惟厥時。」顧茲饑饉荐臻，元元憔悴，公私事力率皆不足。當是時而欲修治水之上策，立不世之奇功，聚大衆，興大役，勞民耗國，困弊立見，曾謂智者而為之乎？然則今日之計何居？相地勢，謹隄防，使河入漕渠而已矣；依故道，去淤澱，使水有蓄洩而已矣。此則漢、宋諸人謂之下策者，然役小費
translation_en:
…the Book on Water Management in Wuzhong proposes first opening the mouth of the Wusong River, relocating the people living on the sandbanks, and cutting openings through the banks at Wujiang to make a thousand bridges. It further proposes opening the Baixian and Anting rivers downstream, so that the waters of Lake Tai can enter the sea by way of Qinglong. Zhao Lin submitted proposals for water management in Pingjiang: first, opening channels and waterways; second, installing sluice gates to regulate the flow; and third, building embankments to enclose fields. These various proposals differ in detail, but all take the intentions of Yu the Great as their guiding principle. Today, low-lying fields frequently suffer flooding, while elevated fields repeatedly suffer drought. If someone could put these proposals into practice on a broader scale, the people's wealth would assuredly be the state's wealth as well.

Nevertheless, there is a time for offering just two ritual vessels of grain, as the Book of Changes states under the hexagram Decrease; and relief from labor obligations takes priority among measures for famine relief. These teachings show that expenditures should be restrained, while people in distress must not go unaided. Fu Yue told Gaozong: “Consider what is good before acting; act only at the proper time.” Yet now famines arrive one after another, the common people are worn down, and public and private resources for undertaking work are generally inadequate. At such a time, if one sought to implement the highest strategy for water management and achieve an extraordinary accomplishment unmatched for generations, gathering great numbers of people and launching vast projects, one would exhaust the people and drain the state; hardship and depletion would immediately follow. Could anyone considered wise do such a thing? What, then, should today's plan be? Simply survey the terrain, attend carefully to the embankments, and direct the river into the grain-transport canal. Simply follow the old channels and remove accumulated silt, so that water can be stored and discharged. These are what the various men of the Han and Song called inferior strategies. Yet the labor required is slight, and the expense…

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
狹固無大利亦無大害也選良吏布膏澤
勞來安輯寬大而不苛靜重而弗擾則民
心悅而和氣應矣和氣應而百順集頌聲
作矣
國家於此何事不可為何功不可建哉抑水
之患非獨茲地而已民之病亦非獨水患
而已
聖主得賢嘉謨贊化日夜講求漸次除治其效
盖可使夷狄賓魚鳥若而況於河患之大
===
乎況於財賦所自出之壤乎執事幸無慮

而已

乎况於財賦所自出之壤乎執事幸無慮
punctuated: 狹，固無大利，亦無大害也。選良吏，布膏澤，勞來安輯，寬大而不苛，靜重而弗擾，則民心悅而和氣應矣。和氣應而百順集，頌聲作矣。國家於此，何事不可為，何功不可建哉？抑水之患，非獨茲地而已；民之病，亦非獨水患而已。聖主得賢，嘉謨贊化，日夜講求，漸次除治，其效盖可使夷狄賓、魚鳥若，而況於河患之大乎？況於財賦所自出之壤乎？執事幸無慮。
translation_en:
…limited in expense: although it offers no great benefit, neither does it cause great harm. Select good officials, bestow generous care, encourage and comfort the people, and bring them peace and security. Be lenient rather than harsh, calm and dignified without causing disturbance; then the people’s hearts will rejoice, and harmonious influences will respond. When these respond, all things will fall into accord, and songs of praise will arise. What undertaking could the state then fail to accomplish? What achievement could it fail to establish?

Yet flooding afflicts more than this region alone, and the people’s sufferings extend beyond flooding alone. If our sagely sovereign obtains worthy men, whose excellent counsels assist his transforming rule, and they deliberate day and night, gradually remedying these troubles, the results may bring even the Yi and Di peoples into submission and the fish and birds into harmony. How much more, then, could they remedy even the great calamities caused by the Yellow River? How much more could they restore the lands from which tax revenues come? May you, honored sir, have no anxiety.

順天府鄉試錄後序

皇明一天下以来，聖聖相承，祗若天道，與賢為治，洪休偉績，輝映無極。雖夫求才路廣，要之得人，無科目比隆。盖其養之豫，選之精，用之至，創繼同一心，先後守一道而不變者，則使之然。猗歟盛哉！乃正德五年秋八月，天下士悉自貢于其鄉，以升如故事，是維成周攷德行道藝、興賢能之意。於是學士臣珪、侍講學士臣澄，並受詔出考京府試。臣澄明不至，亦惟夙夜與
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Since the imperial Ming unified All Under Heaven, sage sovereign has succeeded sage sovereign, reverently following the Way of Heaven and governing together with worthy men. Their abundant blessings and mighty achievements shine without limit. Although the avenues for seeking talent are broad, in obtaining suitable men none equals the examination system in distinction. This results from nurturing them beforehand, selecting them carefully, and employing them to the fullest: founders and successors have shared one purpose, and earlier and later sovereigns have upheld one unchanging Way. Ah, how flourishing!

In the autumn of the fifth year of Zhengde [1510], in the eighth month, scholars throughout the realm presented themselves in their respective home regions for advancement, according to established practice. This embodied the intent of the Zhou dynasty in its flourishing days: to examine virtue, conduct, knowledge of the Way, and accomplishments, and to promote the worthy and capable. Thereupon your servants Gui, Academician, and Cheng, Expositor-in-waiting, both received an imperial command to go out and serve as Examiners for the examination of the capital prefecture. title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
共事之臣慎擇其文理之純者
而取之其限於
制額而不能盡取者姑使需後試
舍是蓋莫可致力者於乎所貴
乎士者獨文藝乎哉今茲所取
百三十五人將來委質吾
君為忠為良必自今日始所以戒飭
===
而期于克終臣烏可以默人之
言曰儒者之學明體而適用若
周之士德行道藝萃于厥躬惟
上所任使是故役萬物應萬變
動而不窮儒者何以能然也學
之至也惟我
國家真有厚望於士士真能無負

百三十五人將來委質吾

言曰儒者之學明體而適用若
周之士德行道藝萃于厥躬惟
上所任使是故役萬物應萬變
動而不窮儒者何以能然也學
之至也惟我
國家眞有厚望於士士眞能無負
punctuated: 共事之臣慎擇其文理之純者而取之，其限於制額而不能盡取者，姑使需後試。舍是，蓋莫可致力者。於乎！所貴乎士者，獨文藝乎哉？今茲所取百三十五人，將來委質吾君，為忠為良，必自今日始。所以戒飭而期于克終，臣烏可以默？人之言曰：「儒者之學，明體而適用。」若周之士，德行道藝萃于厥躬，惟上所任使，是故役萬物，應萬變，動而不窮。儒者何以能然也？學之至也。惟我國家真有厚望於士，士真能無負
translation_en:
…with the officials serving alongside me, carefully selecting and admitting those whose writing and reasoning are sound. Those whom we cannot all admit because of the imperially prescribed quota must for now be left to await a later examination. Beyond this, there is little upon which we can bring our efforts to bear. Alas! Is literary accomplishment alone what we prize in scholars? The 135 men selected on this occasion will in time pledge their service to our sovereign. To become loyal and worthy servants, they must begin this very day. How, then, could I remain silent instead of admonishing them and urging them to persevere to the end?

It has been said: “The learning of the Confucian scholar illuminates fundamental principles and applies them in practice.” The scholars of the Zhou, for example, embodied virtue, conduct, the Way, and the arts, ready for whatever duties their ruler assigned them. Thus they could direct the myriad things and respond to the myriad changes, acting with inexhaustible resourcefulness. How can Confucian scholars achieve this? Through bringing their learning to its fullest extent. Our state indeed places great hopes in its scholars; if those scholars can truly avoid disappointing…

title: 正德五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
國家是使科目之盛有古造士進
士之風而待之重得之榮者也
諸生以
帝畿之秀一日繫其名於賢能之書
而登于
天府天下之士莫先焉道之難知
也名之難成也尚益懋于學充
===
其美質以成大器斯亦庶乎其
可哉且古之人學而仕仕而學
盖終始是事而無窮已臣已仕
者其敢廢學第愧具官碌碌徒
以斯言為未仕者勗也
翰林院侍講學士奉政大夫毛
澄謹序

諸生以

而登于

===
其美質以成大器斯亦庶乎其
可哉且古之人學而仕仕而學
蓋終始是事而無窮已〔臣已仕〕
者其敢廢學第愧具官碌碌徒
以斯言為未仕者勗也
翰林院侍講學士奉政大夫毛
澄謹序
punctuated:
國家，是使科目之盛有古造士、進士之風，而待之重、得之榮者也。諸生以帝畿之秀，一日繫其名於賢能之書，而登于天府，天下之士莫先焉。道之難知也，名之難成也，尚益懋于學，充其美質，以成大器，斯亦庶乎其可哉！且古之人，學而仕，仕而學，盖終始是事而無窮已。臣已仕者，其敢廢學？第愧具官碌碌，徒以斯言為未仕者勗也。
翰林院侍講學士、奉政大夫毛澄謹序。
translation_en:
…the state. This enables the flourishing examination system to embody the spirit of antiquity’s cultivation and advancement of scholars, with the weighty regard in which they are held and the honor they gain. You students, the outstanding talents of the imperial capital region, now have your names entered in the register of the worthy and able and rise to distinction in the capital prefecture; no scholars in the realm stand before you. How difficult it is to understand the Way, and how difficult to establish a reputation! May you strive still harder in learning and develop your fine innate qualities, so as to become men of great capacity. Then you may perhaps approach this ideal!
Moreover, the men of antiquity studied and then entered office; once in office, they continued to study. From beginning to end, they pursued this endeavor without cease. As your servant already holds office, how could I dare abandon learning? I am only ashamed that I occupy my post without distinction, and can merely offer these words as encouragement to those who have yet to enter office.
Preface respectfully composed by Mao Cheng, Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Governance.
